  "target": "flask-app.lab:8015",
  "date": "2026-11-15",
  "findings": [
    {
      "title": "Broken Access Control - Admin Endpoint",
      "endpoint": "/api/admin",
      "severity": "High",
      "evidence": "{\"all_users\":[{\"email\":\"attacker@evil.com\",\"id\":1,\"username\":\"admin\"},{\"email\":\"j.doe@flask-app.lab\",\"id\":2,\"username\":\"j.doe\"},{\"email\":\""
    },
    {
      "title": "IDOR on User Records",
      "endpoint": "/api/v1/users/{id}",
      "severity": "High",
      "evidence": "Enumerated all 4 user accounts using a single non-admin token by incrementing the id parameter"
    },
    {
      "title": "File Upload Content-Type Bypass",
      "endpoint": "/upload",
      "severity": "Critical",
      "evidence": "shell.php uploaded successfully by spoofing Content-Type to image/jpeg"
    },
    {
      "title": "Exposed API Documentation",
      "endpoint": "/apispec_1.json",
      "severity": "Medium",
      "evidence": "Full API schema accessible without authentication, including internal developer comments"
    }
  ]
}

Valid JSON, and notice the \" escaping jq generated automatically inside the evidence string. The lesson: jq -n --arg beats a hand-rolled heredoc every time a value might contain quotes, newlines, or anything else JSON-special — which, in a security-report pipeline full of raw HTTP responses, is most of the time.

Part 2 — Tool Selection Matrix

Tool Wins when Loses when curl Scripting, pipelines, LOTL, low footprint, custom headers, precise control GUI needed, large multi-step state management wget Recursive download, mirroring whole sites Anything beyond downloading HTTPie Human-readable output for quick checks and demos Pipelines, automation, scripting Postman GUI-driven API exploration, sharing collections with a team Engagement scripting, LOTL, low-footprint requirements Python requests Complex logic, stateful workflows, custom parsing, error handling Quick one-liners, environments with no Python interpreter

Part 3 — What This Series Built

Sixteen articles. Five blocks. The skills stack:

  • curl is libcurl — a protocol engine, not a download tool
  • Every flag has a purpose; every combination has an effect
  • URLs have structure; payloads break when you ignore it
  • Responses are intelligence — status codes, headers, timing, body all tell you something
  • Authentication is a scheme — read the challenge, pick the right flag
  • Sessions persist through cookie jars; CSRF tokens are extractable
  • Headers are inputs — they can be manipulated for bypass and recon
  • Burp and curl are complementary; learn to move between them
  • Version strings lead to CVEs through a structured pipeline
  • File operations cover three directions: in, across, and out
  • WAF evasion is about signal reduction, not magic bypasses
  • TLS handshakes contain recon data — read them
  • Bash and jq turn one-liners into pipelines
  • Pivots extend access; curl’s native SOCKS5 is the tool

The value of this series is not any individual technique. It is the mindset: every HTTP interaction is an input/output system, and curl gives you precise control over every part of the input.

This is the end of the series. The lab from this article is open source if you want to run every attack yourself: github.com/roshanrajbanshi/curl-article15-lab. The natural next step beyond that is TryHackMe’s “Web Fundamentals” path every technique from this series applies directly.

Full Chain: Recon to Report with Nothing But curl was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: A Startup’s Guide to Sharding Postgres
partialText:
Intro

Most projects begin with a single Postgres instance for data persistence, and that is the right call. For some of them — for the lucky ones — the data keeps growing until one database becomes expensive and risky to operate. Depending on the workload, there are different answers to scaling the database — sharding is one of them, but outside of system design interviews it is rarely discussed beyond the choice of a sharding key.

We sharded Postgres at the application level for a write-heavy, data-intensive backend. We started with one instance, have since grown to several, and moved data between them while serving users without UX impact. This article covers why we did it, how it works, and what went wrong along the way. It is written for engineers at startups, where the budget matters as much as the architecture.

This article was inspired by The startup’s Postgres survival guide by Alexander Belanger of Hatchet. That guide keeps a single Postgres instance healthy, and this one picks up when a single instance is no longer enough.

Table of Contents

  1. Our Context
  2. How Big Is Too Big
  3. Alternatives We Rejected
  4. Application-Level Sharding
  5. Rebalancing in Production
  6. CDC during Rebalancing
  7. Lessons Learned

Our Context

We are a startup, not a deep-pocketed tech company, so cost and operational complexity drive most of our decisions.

A few words about requirements and the nature of the application’s data:

  • data is naturally partitioned by the user_id with no cross-user_id operations and low risk of hot partitions
  • application is write-skewed
  • writes go through Kafka, keyed by user_id, and a consumer is the only writer to the database
  • every write assigns the row a per-user sequence number in the same transaction, and clients sync incrementally by requesting rows above the last sequence they have seen
  • deletes are soft (except for legal erasure such as GDPR)
  • clients are local-first iOS and Android apps, with many app versions in the wild. They do not need the backend to be useful and may sync overnight while the phone charges, so latency matters little

How Big Is Too Big

Martin Kleppmann, in “Designing Data-Intensive Applications”, calls a system data-intensive when its difficulty comes from the data (its volume, complexity, or rate of change) rather than from computation. I would add that “big” also depends on who is asking. What is big for a startup may be peanuts for an enterprise and a rounding error for Big Tech. For a startup driven by unit economics, a few terabytes of hot transactional data can already be a serious problem.

Many projects start on a single Postgres instance and leave scaling to their future selves. I am guilty of this too: a couple of years ago I designed a project for ever-growing data with warm and cold storage, and cold storage never made it to production. Its largest table has since crossed our operational comfort limit, and the costs, risk, and headaches grew with it. The good news is that this project is moving into the sharded database I’m writing about.

What Breaks First

Postgres has no hard limit on data size. The limits come from the operations around it:

  • Disaster recovery: point-in-time restore of 1TB on AWS can take an hour, plus 1–4 hours of degraded performance while blocks lazily load from S3
  • Vacuum and bloat: VACUUM FULL locks the table for hours, and pg_repack needs free disk for a full copy of the table
  • Schema changes: a humble ALTER COLUMN TYPE can rewrite and lock a huge table for hours
  • Indexes: index rebuilds take hours even with CONCURRENTLY
  • Replication and CDC: replica provisioning takes hours if not days, and a stalled CDC consumer makes the slot hold WAL until it eats the free disk
  • Human errors: a bad migration has a big blast radius

Most of these come down to disk headroom. Vacuum, reindex, ALTER, and a lagging CDC slot all need free space on top of the data, and you often need it only for a few hours. But RDS (assuming you're on AWS) does not let you easily shrink allocated storage, so that headroom becomes a permanent part of your bill. At some point the headroom cost plus the size-dependent risks exceed the cost of one more, smaller instance.

That gives us two limits:

  • The unit of maintenance. Vacuum, reindex, and repack work on one table or partition at a time, so headroom is sized by the largest one. We keep it under 100GB including indexes.
  • The instance. Sooner or later you move half of an instance’s data to a new node (a “rebalance”), and the whole thing (copy, cut-over, clean-up, repack) should fit into one or two days. For us that means at most 1TB including indexes per instance.

We employ different strategies to manage those limits: partitioning to keep the unit of maintenance small and database sharding to keep instance size operationally manageable. We start preparing a rebalance no later than when the largest instance reaches 700GB. Splitting at 700GB leaves two instances of 350GB with plenty of room, while splitting at 950GB leaves 475GB each and another split soon. If you can predict a jump in data volume, say after a feature release, add instances before the data arrives.

Alternatives We Rejected

Scaling Without Sharding

Most of the usual options solve read load or CPU, not the size of one instance under heavy writes. A bigger instance buys CPU and memory, but restore time, vacuum, and headroom still grow with the data. Read replicas scale reads, while every write still lands on one primary and each replica multiplies the storage bill. Partitioning keeps the unit of maintenance small, and we use it for that, but the instance keeps growing. Archiving cold data to a LakeHouse means merging hot and cold data on the read path, with unpredictable latency and painful pagination and deduplication. Housekeeping, like dropping unused indexes, can free a surprising amount of space, but it is not a growth strategy.

NoSQL

Naturally partitioned data with no cross-partition operations makes a NoSQL data model a real option. It is not impossible to build per-user transactional sequencing (a form of the Transactional Outbox Pattern) on NoSQL. I built one on DynamoDB and still maintain it as part of another project. But it comes with hard trade-offs. You either duplicate data (secondary indexes, streams) or accept inefficient reads with several expensive round trips between the application and the database. Each NoSQL engine also brings its own constraints, such as limits on query response size or eventually consistent reads.

Skipping the full trade-off analysis, I’ll cherry-pick the considerations that ruled NoSQL out:

  • DynamoDB storage alone costs about $2.5k/month per 10TB on Standard tables, a Global Secondary Index likely doubles that, and for a write-heavy workload with a transactional sequence update on every write, writes cost even more.
  • Cassandra, which we already run in a legacy project, writes CDC logs per node, so every write shows up once per replica and needs custom deduplication.
  • ScyllaDB recently discontinued its open-source releases, and the license came out comparable to DynamoDB.
  • Finally, I was the only one on the development team with production NoSQL data modeling experience, and that is a risk in itself.

Postgres gave us transactions for the per-user sequence, mature CDC through Debezium, and expertise across the team.

NewSQL / Relational

AWS Aurora bills storage, I/O, and instance hours separately, which makes it hard to predict and expensive for a startup. Its storage does shrink when data is removed, which solves the headroom problem, so run your own numbers.

YugabyteDB looks interesting, but its open-source version could change license as ScyllaDB and CockroachDB did.

PostgreSQL Sharding Solutions

Citus suits distributed queries and cross-shard joins, which we don’t need. It adds a coordinator every query passes through, and RDS does not support it.

PgDog, a sharding proxy with online resharding, is worth watching, but its Sharding 1.0 milestone was 41% done when we looked.

These solutions add a layer for queries that span shards — something we do not need. They also do nothing for disk headroom or operational complexity, and they add a new dependency to manage.

Application-Level Sharding

For the theory and other examples, see:

  • Shard (database architecture)
  • Instagram, Sharding & IDs at Instagram
  • Notion, Herding elephants: lessons learned from sharding Postgres at Notion

With application-level sharding, the application decides which instance to talk to. Given a shard key, a small router (a class in the application code) looks up the instance in a config map, takes a connection from that instance’s pool, and runs the query. Each instance is an ordinary Postgres that has no idea it is part of a cluster.

In return, you own the router, the config, and the rebalancing tooling. There are no cross-shard transactions or joins, every migration runs on every instance, and cross-user analytics moves out of Postgres (for us, into a LakeHouse fed by CDC). When this fits your data model, it is the simplest and most reliable approach, and Instagram and Notion both took it.

The Sharding Key

A good sharding key is present in every query, never changes, and has high cardinality. user_id meets all three. High cardinality still does not guarantee even load: paying users often generate more data, and a shard full of churned users gets quieter while one with new users gets busier. Virtual shards help smooth this out.

Virtual Sharding

We wanted to start with one instance and add more as data grows, without ever moving all or most of the data across instances (a full resharding). Naive sharding, hash(user_id) % N, fails the second goal. Going from N to N+1 instances changes the modulus and moves roughly N/(N+1) of all users.

Virtual shards break the direct link between the key and the instance. Every user_id maps to a fixed virtual shard, hash(user_id) % 512, and a small config maps ranges of virtual shards to physical instances. Adding an instance means moving only the virtual shards assigned to it, and the same mechanism can isolate a hot shard on its own instance. Use a hash that gives the same result in every language and process; we use MurmurHash3 over the string form of user_id.

The router keeps a connection pool per instance and looks up the instance in O(1). The map lives in git and changes through a pull request, and connection strings live in a secret store. A mistake in the map sends writes to the wrong instance, so the application checks on startup that the ranges cover all 512 virtual shards with no gaps or overlaps. If one cluster ever runs out of capacity, several routers can send different groups of users to different clusters.

Every row also stores virtual_shard_id, at two bytes per row. Logical replication filters by it during rebalancing, since Postgres has no built-in MurmurHash3 to compute it on the fly, and the LakeHouse uses it to know which shard a row belongs to.

How many virtual shards
Changing this number means a full resharding, so choose carefully. It caps the number of physical instances and sets how finely you can move data. It should divide evenly by the instance counts you expect. Powers of two divide well by 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and every rebalance can split a range exactly in half, but they divide poorly by 3, 5, or 6. Notion chose 480 because it divides by many small numbers. Our data is spread evenly, so we took 512 and split ranges in half.

To keep the terms straight: rebalancing moves virtual shards between instances and keeps the hash and the shard count. Resharding changes the scheme itself and moves most rows, and we designed the system so we never need it.

Rebalancing in Production

Take the simplest case, adding a second instance to a single-instance cluster. Source holds all 512 virtual shards, and the new Target should take 256–511.

  1. Prepare both instances: provision Target, apply migrations, enable logical replication on Source.
  2. Copy the data from Source to Target with logical replication filtered by virtual_shard_id BETWEEN 256 AND 511.
  3. Settle Target: wait for the initial copy, let the lag drop, refresh statistics.
  4. Cut over: stop writes, wait for zero lag, switch reads and writes for 256–511 to Target, stop replication, resume writes.
  5. Fix index bloat on Target.
  6. Clean up shards 256–511 on Source.

Everything except the cut-over runs with the application fully online. The cut-over is hard because replication must stop exactly when writes start going to Target, and the two cannot be made atomic. We call the time between stopping and resuming writes the cut-over window. Reads keep working during it, but writes wait for a couple of minutes.

Preparation

Most of the risk can be removed before the rebalance starts.

  • Set wal_level = logical (on RDS, rds.logical_replication) well ahead, ideally before production, because it needs a restart. Check max_replication_slots and max_wal_senders, since the rebalance and CDC both need slots.
  • Run the same Postgres major version on both sides.
  • Apply migrations to Target with your usual tooling, and freeze schema changes until the cut-over, because logical replication does not replicate DDL.
  • Give both instances disk headroom for WAL, since replication and CDC slots hold it.
  • Grant the replication user its role and read access only for the rebalance.
  • Make sure you can stop all writers at once: disable their autoscaling and check that queue retention is far longer than the pause.
  • Render scripts for this particular rebalance, so nobody edits SQL by hand during the window, and run the same scripts in integration tests first. Fill in a checklist as you go; it becomes your log and a source of optimization ideas for the next rebalance.

Copying with Logical Replication

We use row-filtered logical replication, available since Postgres 15:

-- on Source
CREATE PUBLICATION rebalance
  FOR TABLE your_table WHERE (virtual_shard_id BETWEEN 256 AND 511)
  WITH (publish_via_partition_root = true);  -- required for partitioned tables
-- on Target
CREATE SUBSCRIPTION rebalance
  CONNECTION 'host=... dbname=... '
  PUBLICATION rebalance
  WITH (copy_data = true);

Set the replica identity first. A row filter on a publication that publishes UPDATE and DELETE may only use columns from the table's replica identity, and the default (the primary key) does not include virtual_shard_id. Postgres does not check this when you create the publication. CREATE PUBLICATION succeeds, and then your application's updates and deletes on Source start failing with "Column used in the publication WHERE expression is not part of the replica identity". So change it before creating the publication:

ALTER TABLE your_table REPLICA IDENTITY FULL;

On partitioned tables, the row filter requires publish_via_partition_root = true, and the replica identity does not propagate from the root, so set it on every partition.

FULL has a price. On Source, every update and delete writes the whole old row to WAL. On Target before Postgres 16, every replicated update and delete finds its row with a sequential scan. The alternative is REPLICA IDENTITY USING INDEX with a unique index that includes virtual_shard_id, which costs one more, very inefficient index. Set REPLICA IDENTITY DEFAULT back on the table and every partition at the cut-over, right after dropping the publication.

copy_data (the default) copies the existing rows before streaming changes. Each table is copied in one long transaction, during which vacuum on Source cannot remove dead rows, and max_sync_workers_per_subscription (2 by default) caps how many tables copy in parallel.

Settling the Target

A table has finished its initial copy when it reaches sync state r:

-- on Target
SELECT srrelid::regclass, srsubstate
FROM pg_subscription_rel
WHERE srsubstate <> 'r';

Measure the lag on Source, not Target. pg_stat_subscription on Target can look healthy while Target is far behind, and the reliable number comes from the replication slot:

-- on Source
SELECT slot_name,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_current_wal_lsn() - confirmed_flush_lsn) AS behind
FROM pg_replication_slots
WHERE slot_name = 'rebalance';

While the application writes, look for a small, stable lag; it reaches zero only after writes stop.

A freshly copied table has no planner statistics, so the first minutes after the cut-over can get really slow. Autovacuum will analyze the tables on its own, but it takes a while, so let it finish before the window. Then check last_analyze and last_autoanalyze in pg_stat_user_tables and run ANALYZE by hand where needed. We learned this the hard way, when running ANALYZE inside the window only made the window longer.

Cut-over

Since stopping replication and switching writes cannot be atomic, you either make sure nothing is written during the switch or make the overlap harmless.

Dual write takes the second route: the application writes the moved shards to both instances while replication runs, and there is no pause. But a row must come out identical on both sides whichever write lands first, so the database cannot compute any value such as now(), an id, or a counter. Our per-user sequence is assigned in the database, which rules dual write out, and it would also double write latency.

Rolling update is a cheaper variant of dual write. Instead of writing to both instances, you roll out the new config gradually: old workers write to Source, which replicates to Target, and new workers write to Target directly. The same condition on writes applies.

Since the per-user sequence rules out both dual write and rolling update, we pause writes. Our local-first clients retry and do not need read-your-writes, and Kafka on the write path buffers writes, so users notice nothing. Without Kafka, rejecting writes for the window would work just as well for a local-first client.

The procedure

1. Stop all writers. Scale the Kafka consumers to zero. Writes pile up in Kafka, reads keep working, and the window starts.

2. Wait for replication to settle. Every table on Target is in state r, and the lag on the Source slot is exactly zero.

3. Switch the shard map with writers still at zero. If writers scale up together with the map change, their writes clash with the still-running replication and fail with duplicate key errors.

4. Stop replication. On Target, detach the subscription from its slot first, so the drop does not need a connection to Source:

ALTER SUBSCRIPTION rebalance DISABLE;
ALTER SUBSCRIPTION rebalance SET (slot_name = NONE);
DROP SUBSCRIPTION rebalance;

Then drop the publication and the slot on Source, and set REPLICA IDENTITY DEFAULT back.

5. Resume writers. The consumers drain the Kafka backlog into Target, and the window ends.

Step 5 is the point of no return. Until then, you roll back by reverting the map, because Source still has every row. Once consumers write to Target, Source falls behind, and going back would need replication in the opposite direction. That is why the map switch and the writer restart are separate changes.

After Cut-over: Index Bloat

After the copy, indexes on Target were up to twice the size of the same index built from scratch. copy_data inserts rows into tables whose indexes already exist. With random keys, such as UUIDs or hash-based deduplication keys, each insert lands on a random B-tree leaf, full pages split in half, and the halves never fill up again. An index built in one pass from sorted data packs its pages densely.

The fix is a rebuild:

REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY your_table_pkey;

CONCURRENTLY keeps the table available, but it needs free disk for a full copy of the index, takes hours on large ones, and writes a lot of WAL for your CDC slot to process. Rebuild one index at a time, estimate the gain first with pgstatindex from pgstattuple, and check the result with pg_relation_size. We do this after the cut-over, because bloat does not affect correctness and every hour of replication piles up WAL on Source.

Clean-up

After the cut-over, Source still holds every row of the moved shards — they have to be cleaned. This sounds like the easy part, but it turned out to be the hardest: we delete a large share of the rows in the biggest tables.

We have no index on virtual_shard_id and do not want one, given its size and low selectivity, so finding the rows means scanning the table. Naive batching, DELETE ... WHERE virtual_shard_id BETWEEN ... LIMIT n in a loop, degrades. Each batch scans from the start of the table past more and more dead rows, until a batch takes many minutes. VACUUM between batches helps only for a while.

Instead, we batch by physical location. Every row has a ctid (block number and position in the block), and since Postgres 14 a ctid range runs as a Tid Range Scan that reads only those blocks. So we walk the table in fixed chunks of blocks, one transaction per chunk:

DELETE FROM your_table
WHERE ctid >= '(0,0)'::tid AND ctid < '(512,0)'::tid
  AND virtual_shard_id BETWEEN 256 AND 511;
-- next batch: (512,0) .. (1024,0), and so on up to the last block

Each batch now costs about the same, so the total time is predictable.

Watch the WAL. Every deleted row goes to WAL, and the CDC slot holds it until the consumer chews through millions of delete events. If you delete faster than CDC consumes, WAL eats the free disk. Throttle the batches and pause when the slot lag grows; we had to stop and resume several times.

Watch autovacuum. Mass deletes trigger autovacuum, which competes for I/O and writes WAL of its own. Disabling it in the RDS parameter group did not work for us, only the per-table setting did:

ALTER TABLE your_table SET (autovacuum_enabled = false);
-- and back to true when the clean-up is done

Even that is not a guarantee. In one rebalance, vacuum started anyway mid-clean-up, and together they pushed disk usage past the RDS storage autoscaling threshold. Keep an eye on the RDS I/O burst balance as well, because draining it degrades performance.

Don’t expect the disk back. Postgres reuses the freed space for new rows, but the files do not shrink. That is fine for us, because Source grows back into the space it already pays for.

Another option
Some applications can make virtual_shard_id the first column of the primary key:
PRIMARY KEY (virtual_shard_id, id)
Then both the clean-up and the replication filter get an index for free. But this affects query design, index size, foreign keys, uniqueness and deduplication, ORM support, and CDC.

CDC during Rebalancing

Every instance streams changes to our LakeHouse with Debezium through its own slot. The LakeHouse should not notice a rebalance: the copy must not look like new data, the hand-over must leave no gaps or duplicates, and the clean-up must not look like deletes.

Start CDC on Target inside the cut-over window. A CDC slot on Target during the copy would emit every copied row as an insert, millions of duplicates. So we create it after the lag reaches zero and before writers resume. Every change before that point reached the LakeHouse through Source, and every change after it comes through Target. The write pause gives us this boundary for free. Target’s Debezium connector also runs with snapshot.mode = never, since a default snapshot would cause the same flood.

Rewrite row ownership. Each LakeHouse record carries the instance it came from, so after the cut-over we update that attribute for the moved shards.

Ignore the clean-up deletes. Soft deletes make this easy. Physical deletes in the stream come only from the clean-up or from legal erasure, which purges the LakeHouse through its own process, so CDC can safely skip them. Without soft deletes, it would need to know which shards moved and drop their deletes from Source.

Mind the WAL on Source. Until the cut-over, Source has two slots holding WAL, and REPLICA IDENTITY FULLmakes every change heavier. In a non-production rehearsal, WAL grew far more than we expected, and we had to drop the CDC connector and restore it later. Since then we watch both slots as closely as free disk.

Lessons Learned

  • Shard from day one, even on one instance. A router, virtual shards, and a virtual_shard_id column cost almost nothing when data is small, and retrofitting them is a project of its own.
  • Shrink the cut-over window. Only replication catch-up, the config switch, and stopping replication need stopped writes, and each of our rebalances kept less inside the window.
  • Plan by the clean-up. The copy takes hours and the cut-over minutes, but the clean-up takes days.
  • Storage autoscaling is a one-way door. A short spike during clean-up becomes a permanent cost.
  • Not every growth problem needs a new instance. Rebuild bloated indexes first, or move virtual shards between existing instances.
  • Forecast, don’t react. The active part of a rebalance takes a couple of days, but planning, alignment, and infrastructure setup take weeks of calendar time, so track the largest instance’s monthly growth.
  • Prefer writes the application controls. Soft deletes and app-computed values keep CDC simple and dual write possible.
  • Run Postgres 16 or newer. Row filters need 15, and 16 lets the subscriber use indexes for tables with REPLICA IDENTITY FULL.
  • Test with several databases. Cover the shard router and rebalance process with integration tests that run against several instances. Make sure your rebalance integration tests use exactly the same scripts as the real rebalance, so the runbook and scripts are proven. Rehearse the first rebalance while the data is small.
  • One size doesn’t fit all. If your clients need read-your-writes, or you have hard deletes and non-idempotent writes, a simple write pause may not be enough.

Recommended Reading

Books

  • Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann and Chris Riccomini (2nd edition, O’Reilly, 2026). The chapters on replication, sharding, and stream processing explain the theory behind virtual shards, rebalancing, and CDC.
  • Software Architecture: The Hard Parts by Neal Ford, Mark Richards, Pramod Sadalage, and Zhamak Dehghani (O’Reilly, 2021). It covers how to pull apart operational data and weigh the trade-offs of distributed data ownership.
  • NoSQL Distilled: A Brief Guide to the Emerging World of Polyglot Persistence by Pramod Sadalage and Martin Fowler (Addison-Wesley, 2012). It is a short introduction to distribution models, sharding, and consistency trade-offs. Martin Fowler’s Polyglot Persistence note explains the idea in the title.
  • PostgreSQL 14 Internals by Egor Rogov (Postgres Professional, 2023, free PDF). It explains MVCC, vacuum, WAL, and index internals, which is where bloat and replication behavior come from.

Articles

  • Herding elephants: lessons learned from sharding Postgres at Notion by Garrett Fidalgo (Notion, 2021). Notion sharded Postgres in the application with logical shards and moved data with a dual write and a backfill.
  • The Great Re-shard: adding Postgres capacity (again) with zero downtime by Arka Ganguli, Tanner Johnson, Ben Kraft, and Nathan Northcutt (Notion, 2023). The follow-up post moves logical shards to new instances with logical replication, close to the rebalancing described here.
  • How Figma’s databases team lived to tell the scale by Sammy Steele (Figma, 2024). Figma took a different path and built horizontal sharding into a query proxy in front of Postgres.

How smaller models help larger LLMs generate tokens faster without compromising output quality.

Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have become remarkably capable, but generating responses quickly remains one of the biggest challenges in deploying them at scale.

When you ask ChatGPT a question, the model doesn’t generate the entire response in one operation. It generates tokens sequentially, one after another. Each new token depends on the tokens generated before it.

This process is called autoregressive decoding.

Although autoregressive generation produces high-quality results, it introduces a significant performance bottleneck: the model must repeatedly execute inference to generate every token.

Imagine an LLM generating a response containing 500 tokens. In a conventional decoding process, it may need approximately 500 sequential decoding iterations.

What if we could generate several tokens at once, verify whether they are correct, and accept the valid ones without compromising the output distribution?

That’s precisely the idea behind Speculative Decoding.

Speculative decoding is an inference optimization technique that uses a smaller, faster draft model to propose multiple tokens, while a larger target model verifies those proposals in parallel. Instead of waiting for the target model to generate every token individually, we allow it to validate several potential tokens in a single forward pass.

The result can be significantly faster inference while preserving the target model’s original probability distribution.

In this article, we’ll explore how speculative decoding works, its architecture, mathematical foundations, implementation strategies, performance trade-offs, and practical applications.

The Problem: Why Is LLM Inference Slow?

To understand speculative decoding, we first need to understand how traditional LLM inference works.

Autoregressive token generation

Most modern decoder-only LLMs generate text using an autoregressive process.

Given an input sequence, the model predicts the probability distribution of the next token.

For example, consider the prompt:

The capital of France is

The model selects a token, appends it to the sequence, and runs the next decoding step.

The process repeats until the response is complete.

Why sequential generation creates latency

There are three important factors.

1. Sequential dependency

The next token cannot be generated until the previous token has been selected. This creates a sequential dependency that limits parallelism during decoding.

2. Memory bandwidth bottleneck

During batch-size-one inference, the GPU often needs to repeatedly load model weights from memory to perform relatively little computation per generated token.

For large models, this can make inference memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound.

3. Repeated model execution

Even when generating a relatively short response, the target model must perform repeated decoding steps.

For example:

The challenge is not necessarily that GPUs cannot process tokens quickly. It is that autoregressive decoding limits how much useful work can be performed in parallel.

Speculative decoding attempts to overcome this limitation.

What Is Speculative Decoding?

Speculative decoding is a technique that accelerates autoregressive LLM inference by separating token generation into two roles:

  • Draft model: A smaller, faster model that predicts multiple future tokens.
  • Target model: The larger, more capable model that verifies the proposed tokens.

The draft model makes predictions about what the target model is likely to generate. The target model then evaluates these predictions together rather than generating each token independently.

The central insight is simple:

It is often cheaper to verify several tokens in parallel than to generate those tokens sequentially.

The two-model architecture

The process works as follows:

  1. The user submits a prompt.
  2. The draft model predicts several future tokens.
  3. The target model evaluates all proposed tokens in a parallel verification pass.
  4. Matching tokens are accepted.
  5. At the first mismatch, the target model generates an appropriate replacement.
  6. The process continues from the updated sequence.

This means a single target-model execution can potentially produce multiple committed output tokens.

That is where the latency savings come from.

How Does Speculative Decoding Work Internally?

Let’s understand the complete execution cycle.

Step 1: Draft generation

The draft model receives the existing prompt and generates a sequence of candidate tokens.

For example:

prompt = "Artificial intelligence is"

draft_tokens = [
    "transforming",
    "modern",
    "businesses",
    "rapidly"
]

The draft model generates these tokens autoregressively, but because it is smaller, each individual generation step is relatively inexpensive.

The number of candidate tokens generated in each cycle is commonly represented by k, the speculation length or draft length.

Step 2: Parallel verification

This is a critical distinction:

  • The draft model generates tokens sequentially.
  • The target model verifies the proposed sequence in parallel.

The target model is not simply predicting four independent tokens. It evaluates each token conditioned on the preceding proposed tokens.

Step 3: Acceptance and rejection

Once the target model evaluates the candidates, the system determines which tokens can be committed.

There are two important decoding scenarios.

Greedy decoding

When using greedy decoding, a drafted token is accepted if it matches the target model’s highest-probability token at that position.

The first mismatch is replaced with the target model’s preferred token.

Sampling-based decoding

When using temperature sampling, top-p, or other probabilistic sampling strategies, simply checking whether the draft token matches the target model’s most likely token would be incorrect.

Instead, speculative decoding uses a mathematically designed acceptance-rejection mechanism. This is what allows it to preserve the target model’s original output distribution.

Step 4: Continue generation

After accepting the valid tokens and correcting the first rejected token, the system updates the sequence and KV cache.

A new speculation cycle begins from the updated context. This process repeats until the model reaches its stopping condition.

The draft model can therefore propose tokens, but the target model retains control over which proposals are committed.

What happens when a token is rejected?

This is the most important part of the algorithm.

When a token is rejected, the system samples a replacement from the residual probability distribution:

The residual distribution captures probability mass that the target model assigns beyond what the draft model proposed.

The replacement is sampled from this distribution, not simply chosen as the target model’s highest-probability token.

This correction is what makes the sampling process mathematically exact.

Why output quality does not degrade

The acceptance rule and residual correction together ensure that the next committed token follows the target distribution.

In other words:

Under the standard algorithm’s assumptions, speculative decoding produces the same probability distribution as ordinary target-model sampling.

This does not mean every generated response will be identical across separate runs. Random sampling can still produce different outputs. It means speculative decoding does not introduce a change in the target distribution.

This distinction is extremely important when evaluating inference optimization techniques.

Why Does Speculative Decoding Reduce Latency?

The real advantage comes from how modern GPUs execute workloads.

Memory bandwidth versus compute utilization

Large language models contain billions of parameters. During autoregressive decoding, the model repeatedly accesses its weights to generate individual tokens.

At low batch sizes, GPU execution can be constrained by memory bandwidth. However, when verifying several candidate tokens together, the target model performs more useful computation for each weight load.

This improves hardware utilization and can make the additional verification work relatively inexpensive.

Comparing the two approaches

Consider a simplified example where a model needs to generate eight tokens.

Instead of eight target-model decoding passes, the second approach requires two verification passes, assuming all proposed tokens are accepted.

Actual performance depends on draft latency, acceptance rate, target-model verification cost, and serving conditions.

The speedup equation

Let:

  • k = number of drafted tokens.
  • α = probability of accepting a draft token.
  • t_d = average draft-model time per token.
  • t_v(k) = target-model verification time for \(k\) draft tokens.
  • E[A] = expected number of output tokens committed per cycle.

where t_T is the latency of one conventional target-model decoding step.

This is a simplified analytical model, not a universal performance guarantee. Real systems must account for KV-cache management, batching, communication, scheduling, and other overheads.

How acceptance rate affects performance

Let’s explore how acceptance probability affects expected tokens per verification cycle.

The graph reveals an important observation:

Higher acceptance rates generally translate into more output tokens per target-model verification pass.

However, maximizing acceptance rate alone is not sufficient. A draft model that is expensive to execute can eliminate the benefits of speculative decoding.

This brings us to one of the most important engineering decisions: choosing the right drafting strategy.

Different Types of Speculative Decoding

The original speculative decoding approach uses a separate draft model. However, researchers have developed several alternatives to reduce drafting overhead and improve acceptance rates.

Here are some important approaches.

Standard speculative decoding

Separate draft model

This is the traditional approach.

A smaller language model generates candidate tokens, and the larger model verifies them.

Advantages

  • Works with existing language models.
  • No modification to the target model is necessarily required.
  • Can preserve the target model’s output distribution.
  • Relatively straightforward to understand and implement.

Limitations

  • Requires an additional model.
  • Draft generation adds computational overhead.
  • Performance depends heavily on draft-target compatibility.

Self-speculative decoding

Single-model approach

Instead of maintaining a separate draft model, the target model itself performs both drafting and verification.

One approach is to use an early exit from intermediate Transformer layers to produce preliminary predictions.

The remaining layers then verify or refine those predictions.

For example:

  • Early Transformer layers produce candidate predictions.
  • Later Transformer layers provide more accurate predictions.
  • The system verifies candidate tokens and commits valid ones.

This approach can reduce the memory overhead of loading and maintaining a separate draft model.

However, it generally requires architectural support or additional implementation work.

Medusa: Multiple decoding heads

Multi-head prediction

One of the interesting developments in speculative decoding is Medusa.

Introduced by researchers in 2024, Medusa adds multiple prediction heads to an existing language model.

Instead of predicting only the next token, these heads attempt to predict multiple future tokens simultaneously.

For example:

  • Head 1 predicts the next token.
  • Head 2 predicts the token after that.
  • Head 3 predicts a further future token.
  • Additional heads predict longer continuations.

The system constructs a tree of candidate continuations and uses tree-based attention to verify them. This is particularly interesting because it avoids maintaining an entirely separate autoregressive draft model.

Why Medusa matters

  • Reduces dependency on an external draft model.
  • Generates multiple candidate continuations.
  • Uses tree-based verification.
  • Can improve inference performance without changing the fundamental autoregressive output objective.

EAGLE: Extrapolation Algorithm for Greater Language-model Efficiency

EAGLE takes a different approach.

Rather than directly predicting future tokens using only token-level information, it uses the target model’s internal feature representations to help draft future tokens.

The idea is that intermediate model features can contain richer information about future token predictions than the token alone.

Its general workflow:

  1. Extract useful internal representations from the target model.
  2. Use a lightweight drafting mechanism to extrapolate future representations.
  3. Predict candidate tokens from those representations.
  4. Verify candidates using the target model.
  5. Accept valid tokens and repeat.

This can improve drafting accuracy while avoiding the need for a conventional independent language model.

Comparison of major approaches

These approaches represent different ways to solve the same problem: generate useful future-token candidates cheaply enough that verification is worthwhile.

Dynamic Speculation: Why Fixed Draft Length Is Not Always Optimal

One of the biggest mistakes in implementing speculative decoding is assuming that the draft model should always generate the same number of tokens.

For example, suppose we always generate five draft tokens.

What happens if the first token is rejected?

The remaining four predictions are no longer useful for that verification cycle. On the other hand, if the first four tokens are consistently accepted, perhaps we should generate more candidates.

This is where dynamic speculation becomes valuable.

Adaptive draft length

Instead of fixing k, the inference engine adjusts the number of draft tokens based on observed acceptance behavior.

For example:

The controller continuously monitors:

  • Token acceptance rate.
  • Average accepted tokens per verification.
  • Draft-model latency.
  • Target-model verification latency.
  • Current GPU utilization.

It then adjusts the speculation budget.

Why this is important?

Different prompts have different levels of predictability.

Consider these two examples:

Example A: Predictable text

“The sun rises in the…”

The next tokens are relatively predictable.

A draft model might achieve a high acceptance rate.

Example B: Complex reasoning

“Calculate the optimal allocation under these five constraints…”

The next tokens may be much harder to predict.

A draft model may frequently propose tokens that the target model rejects.

An adaptive controller can respond to these differences rather than wasting resources on unnecessarily long drafts.

Implementing Speculative Decoding: A Practical Engineering Perspective

Let’s move from theory to implementation.

Suppose we have:

  • Target model: a 70B parameter LLM.
  • Draft model: a compatible 1B parameter LLM.
  • Draft length: five tokens.
  • Inference hardware: GPU accelerator.
  • Serving engine: an inference runtime supporting speculative decoding.

The architecture looks like this:

High-level implementation

The following Python-style pseudocode demonstrates the basic algorithmic structure. It is illustrative rather than a complete production implementation.

def speculative_decode(
    prompt,
    draft_model,
    target_model,
    max_tokens,
    draft_length=5
):
    output = prompt

    while len(output) < max_tokens:

        # Step 1: Generate candidate tokens
        draft_tokens = draft_model.generate(
            output,
            max_new_tokens=draft_length
        )

        # Step 2: Verify candidates in parallel
        target_distributions = target_model.verify(
            output,
            draft_tokens
        )

        accepted = []

        # Step 3: Check each candidate
        for token, target_dist in zip(
            draft_tokens,
            target_distributions
        ):

            if matches_target_rule(token, target_dist):
                accepted.append(token)
            else:
                # Replace first rejected token
                replacement = sample_target(
                    target_dist
                )

                accepted.append(replacement)
                break

        # Step 4: Commit accepted sequence
        output = append_tokens(output, accepted)

    return output

For greedy decoding, matches_target_rule checks the target model's preferred token.

For exact probabilistic sampling, the implementation must use the acceptance ratio and residual distribution described earlier. The pseudocode intentionally abstracts away those details, KV-cache synchronization, and bonus-token handling.

Implementing it using vLLM

For production deployments, using an inference engine with native speculative decoding support is generally preferable to implementing the entire mechanism yourself.

vllm serve <target-model> \
  --speculative-config \
  '{"method":"draft_model",
    "model":"<draft-model>",
    "num_speculative_tokens":5}'

The exact configuration and supported methods depend on the vLLM version, model architecture, and backend.

Relevant implementation considerations include:

  • Draft and target tokenizer compatibility.
  • GPU memory availability.
  • KV-cache management.
  • Parallel verification kernels.
  • Speculation length.
  • Batch size and request scheduling.

Useful implementation resources:

  • vLLM documentation
  • vLLM GitHub repository
  • NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM

Performance Trade-offs and Limitations

Speculative decoding is not a universal solution for every inference workload. Its performance depends on multiple interacting variables.

Draft model quality

A draft model that frequently disagrees with the target model will have a low acceptance rate.

However, a smaller model is not necessarily better simply because it has fewer parameters.

The important metric is how much useful drafting it delivers relative to its execution cost.

A 2025 study, Decoding Speculative Decoding, found that draft-model latency strongly influences performance, and that general language-modeling capability does not necessarily predict speculative decoding effectiveness.

Additional GPU memory

Using a separate draft model requires additional memory.

For example, deploying a 70B target model alongside a 1B draft model requires accommodating both models, their runtime state, and associated KV caches.

This can reduce the available memory for batching and concurrent requests.

High batch-size workloads

At low batch sizes, a large model may be limited by memory bandwidth, making parallel verification attractive.

At high batch sizes, the GPU may already be highly utilized.

The extra computation involved in verifying multiple tokens can then reduce the benefit.

Unpredictable outputs

Some tasks are inherently difficult for draft models:

  • Complex mathematical reasoning.
  • Unusual code generation.
  • Long-form technical reasoning.
  • Highly constrained outputs.
  • Rare vocabulary and domain-specific terminology.

In such cases, acceptance rates may be lower.

Prefill versus decoding

Speculative decoding primarily targets autoregressive generation latency.

It does not inherently solve prompt-processing latency.

Remember that LLM inference has two distinct phases:

This distinction matters when optimizing end-to-end application latency.

How Should We Benchmark Speculative Decoding?

A common mistake is evaluating speculative decoding only through its token acceptance rate. Acceptance rate is useful, but it doesn’t tell us whether the deployment is actually faster.

A proper evaluation should include the following metrics.

Recommended benchmarking methodology

  1. Establish a baseline using the target model without speculation.
  2. Run speculative decoding with the same target model.
  3. Keep prompts, output lengths, sampling settings, hardware, and serving conditions comparable.
  4. Test multiple draft lengths.
  5. Measure both single-user latency and multi-user throughput.
  6. Repeat across different workload categories.
  7. Compare p50, p95, and p99 latency.
  8. Measure actual infrastructure cost.

The most important question is not whether speculative decoding accepts many tokens.

It is whether the additional tokens generated per verification pass outweigh the cost of drafting and verification.

The Future of Speculative Decoding

Speculative decoding is evolving from a relatively simple draft-and-verify technique into a broader family of inference optimization strategies.

Several research directions are particularly interesting.

Multi-token prediction

Future models may be trained to predict multiple future tokens more effectively.

Rather than relying on an independently trained draft model, the target architecture itself could learn to generate useful future-token candidates.

Hardware-aware speculation

The optimal speculation strategy depends on GPU architecture, memory bandwidth, compute capacity, and model size.

Future inference engines will increasingly optimize speculation dynamically based on available hardware resources.

Adaptive inference engines

Inference engines could automatically determine:

  • Whether speculative decoding should be enabled.
  • Which draft model to use.
  • How many tokens to speculate.
  • When to increase or decrease draft length.
  • Which verification strategy is most efficient.

This could make speculative decoding an intelligent runtime optimization rather than a manually configured feature.

Speculative decoding for agentic AI

As AI agents become more sophisticated, they will increasingly rely on repeated reasoning, planning, and tool-selection operations.

Reducing inference latency across these repeated model calls could make agentic systems more responsive.

Combining speculative decoding with efficient KV-cache management, quantization, batching, and optimized agent orchestration could create substantial system-level improvements.

Conclusion

Speculative decoding represents an important shift in how we think about LLM inference optimization.

Traditionally, the approach to faster inference has been to make models smaller, quantize their weights, optimize attention mechanisms, or use faster hardware.

Speculative decoding introduces a different idea: instead of making the target model generate faster one token at a time, make it generate multiple verified tokens per execution cycle.

This is a particularly powerful idea because it exploits an important characteristic of modern GPU inference: processing several known token positions together can be more efficient than repeatedly processing one position at a time.

The technique is not without trade-offs. Draft-model overhead, token acceptance, GPU memory, and workload characteristics determine whether it actually improves performance.

Nevertheless, as LLM applications move toward longer responses, real-time conversational systems, and increasingly autonomous AI agents, speculative decoding will remain an important tool in the inference optimization toolbox.

Ultimately, the future of efficient AI inference will not depend on a single optimization. It will come from combining better architectures, smarter decoding strategies, and hardware-aware execution systems.

Further Reading and Research Papers

These are useful resources for understanding the research behind speculative decoding.

  1. Original speculative decoding paper (2023): Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding — Leviathan, Kalman and Matias.
  2. Speculative sampling (2023): Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling — Chen et al.
  3. Comprehensive survey (2024): Unlocking Efficiency in Large Language Model Inference — Xia et al.
  4. Medusa (2024): Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads.
  5. Online Speculative Decoding (2024): Online Speculative Decoding.
  6. Decoding Speculative Decoding (2025): A detailed empirical study of draft-model efficiency

title: Neuromorphic Computing and Its Applications in AI
partialText:
How brain-inspired computing could transform the future of intelligent machines

Introduction

What if computers could process information more like the human brain rather than repeatedly moving enormous amounts of data between memory and processors?

Modern AI has achieved extraordinary breakthroughs in language understanding, computer vision, robotics and generative AI. However, these capabilities come with a significant cost: computational complexity, energy consumption and hardware requirements.

Training and running increasingly sophisticated AI models requires powerful GPUs, large memory systems and substantial electricity.

But biological intelligence operates differently.

The human brain contains approximately 86 billion neurons connected through trillions of synapses. It processes information through massively parallel, event-driven electrical and chemical signals while consuming roughly 20 watts of power.

This remarkable efficiency has inspired a new computing paradigm: Neuromorphic Computing.

Instead of simply making conventional processors faster, neuromorphic computing rethinks how hardware processes information. It combines principles from neuroscience, computer architecture and artificial intelligence to build systems that behave more like biological neural networks.

The potential applications range from autonomous robots and intelligent sensors to real-time computer vision, healthcare, industrial automation and energy-efficient edge AI.

In this article, we will explore how neuromorphic computing works, its underlying architecture, spiking neural networks, leading hardware platforms, practical AI applications and the challenges that must be solved before it becomes mainstream.

What Is Neuromorphic Computing?

Neuromorphic computing is a computing paradigm inspired by the structure and functioning of the human nervous system.

The term neuromorphic combines two ideas:

  • Neuro: Inspired by biological neurons and synapses.
  • Morphic: Referring to the structure or form of something.

The concept was introduced by Carver Mead in the late 1980s and early 1990s, when he explored how electronic circuits could reproduce aspects of biological neural computation.

Traditional computers separate processing and memory. Neuromorphic systems attempt to bring these functions closer together, using networks of artificial neurons and synapses to process information in parallel.

The fundamental idea is simple:

Instead of continuously processing every input, a neuromorphic system can remain relatively inactive until meaningful information arrives.

For example, consider a conventional security camera monitoring an empty corridor.

A traditional computer vision system might continuously capture frames and run object detection, even when nothing changes.

A neuromorphic vision system can instead detect changes in light intensity and generate events only when something meaningful happens.

If a person walks into the corridor, the sensor produces events corresponding to the movement. The processing system can react without repeatedly analyzing every pixel in every video frame.

This event-driven approach can significantly reduce unnecessary computation.

Key characteristics

  1. Event-driven computation: Processing happens when neurons receive or generate meaningful signals.
  2. Massive parallelism: Many neurons process information simultaneously.
  3. Co-located memory and computation: Synaptic information can be stored close to processing elements.
  4. Sparse communication: Neurons communicate using discrete spikes rather than continuously transmitting dense numerical values.
  5. Asynchronous processing: Different parts of the system can operate independently without requiring a global clock.
  6. Adaptive learning: Certain architectures support learning and changing connections based on incoming signals.

Neuromorphic computing is not simply an attempt to reproduce the entire human brain. It selectively borrows biological principles to solve computational problems more efficiently.

Why Do We Need Neuromorphic Computing?

To understand its importance, we first need to examine the limitations of conventional computing architectures.

The Von Neumann bottleneck

Most conventional computers follow the Von Neumann architecture. It separates the processor and memory into different components. When a processor needs to perform an operation, it retrieves information from memory, processes it and potentially writes the result back. This constant movement of data creates a performance and energy bottleneck.

For modern AI workloads, moving data can be a significant contributor to energy consumption.

For example, when running a deep neural network, the system repeatedly transfers model weights, activations and intermediate results between memory and processing units.

Neuromorphic architectures address this problem by bringing memory and computation closer together. Biological neurons do not operate like conventional CPUs. Synaptic connections store information locally, and neurons communicate through electrical spikes.

This offers an alternative to the traditional processor-memory model.

Traditional vs neuromorphic computing

The distinction is architectural rather than absolute. Modern GPUs also support parallel computation, and not every neuromorphic processor implements every biological characteristic.

The energy-efficiency opportunity

The motivation behind neuromorphic computing becomes clearer when considering the growing demand for AI inference.

A large AI system may need thousands of accelerators, extensive cooling infrastructure and continuous power.

However, many edge applications have very different requirements.

A wearable device, autonomous drone or industrial sensor might need to make decisions continuously while operating on a tiny battery.

Neuromorphic computing is particularly interesting in these situations because it can avoid unnecessary computation when inputs are inactive.

The objective is not to replace GPUs everywhere. It is to develop a more efficient computing architecture for workloads where sparse, asynchronous and real-time processing offers an advantage.

How Does Neuromorphic Computing Work?

The architecture of a neuromorphic system is inspired by three fundamental biological components:

  • Neurons
  • Synapses
  • Electrical spikes

Artificial neurons

A biological neuron receives signals from other neurons through dendrites.

When its membrane potential reaches a particular threshold, it generates an electrical impulse called an action potential.

This impulse travels along the axon and influences other neurons.

Neuromorphic hardware reproduces this behavior using mathematical models and electronic circuits.

One widely used model is the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neuron.

The neuron accumulates incoming signals over time. Its internal potential gradually decreases when it receives no input. When the potential reaches a threshold, the neuron generates a spike and resets its potential.

After generating a spike, its membrane potential is reset.

This simple mechanism allows networks of neurons to process temporal information.

Synapses

Synapses connect neurons and determine how strongly one neuron influences another.

In artificial neuromorphic systems, synaptic weights control the influence of incoming spikes.

For example:

  • Positive weights can excite a neuron.
  • Negative weights can inhibit a neuron.
  • Different weights represent different connection strengths.

When a spike arrives, its corresponding synaptic weight contributes to the receiving neuron’s membrane potential.

This creates a network of interacting computational units.

Spikes: The language of neuromorphic systems

Unlike conventional neural networks that typically process numerical activations through matrix multiplication, spiking neural networks communicate using discrete events.

Information can be represented through:

  • Spike frequency
  • Spike timing
  • Temporal patterns
  • Relative timing between neurons

This makes spiking neural networks particularly suitable for problems involving time-dependent information, such as audio, motion and sensor streams.

Understanding Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs)

Spiking Neural Networks are one of the most important computational models used in neuromorphic computing.

Traditional artificial neural networks generally use continuous-valued activations. For example, a neuron might output 0.72 after applying an activation function. An SNN instead communicates using spikes occurring at particular points in time.

The timing and frequency of these spikes carry information.

ANN vs SNN

Consider an image recognition task.

A conventional ANN receives an image, converts it into numerical values and processes it through multiple layers.

An SNN can encode visual information into spike trains and process those events over time.

The difference is not merely how information is represented. It also changes how computation is scheduled.

How does an SNN process information?

Imagine a robot equipped with an event-based camera.

  1. The camera detects changes in brightness.
  2. These changes are encoded into spikes.
  3. The spikes enter an SNN.
  4. Neurons integrate incoming signals.
  5. Neurons generate new spikes when their thresholds are reached.
  6. The output network recognizes a movement or object.
  7. The robot responds accordingly.

The system can react to changes without continuously processing redundant information.

Training SNNs

Training is one of the most interesting aspects of neuromorphic AI.

Unlike conventional neural networks, SNNs have discontinuous spike-generation functions, making standard gradient-based optimization difficult.

Several approaches are used:

1. Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity (STDP)

A biologically inspired learning rule that adjusts synaptic weights based on the relative timing of pre-synaptic and post-synaptic spikes.

If a pre-synaptic neuron fires shortly before a post-synaptic neuron, the connection may become stronger. The opposite timing relationship may weaken it.

2. Surrogate Gradient Learning

The non-differentiable spike function is approximated during backpropagation using a smooth surrogate function.

This makes gradient-based training possible.

3. ANN-to-SNN Conversion

A previously trained artificial neural network is converted into a spiking neural network.

This allows researchers to reuse conventional deep-learning training techniques, although conversion may introduce accuracy, latency and implementation trade-offs.

4. Local Learning

Some architectures use local learning rules that update synapses without requiring global backpropagation.

This can be useful for adaptive and continuously learning systems.

Neuromorphic Computing Architecture

A neuromorphic computing system typically consists of multiple interconnected layers.

The major components

Input layer: Receives information from sensors, cameras, microphones or other event-generating devices.

Encoding layer: Converts incoming signals into spike-based representations.

Neuron layer: Contains artificial neurons that integrate incoming events and generate spikes.

Synaptic network: Stores connection weights and determines how signals propagate.

Learning mechanism: Updates weights through mechanisms such as STDP or surrogate-gradient-based training.

Output layer: Converts network activity into predictions, classifications or control signals.
